about: A shared UK-wide revision pack for the molecular and cellular science taught in the early, preclinical years of medicine: cell structure, membranes and transport, proteins and enzymes, carbohydrate, lipid and amino acid metabolism, DNA and gene expression, cell signalling and the cell cycle, and inheritance and medical genetics. It is not one university's syllabus, so check your own course's learning outcomes; it is pitched at preclinical level and links each topic to the conditions it explains, with genetics and genomics aligned to the GMC's MLA content map. It is educational material, not clinical advice, and gives no drug doses.
topics: Cell signalling and the cell cycle

notes.h: Eukaryotic cell structure: organelles and the cytoskeleton
notes.overview: Eukaryotic cells divide their work between membrane-bound compartments and a protein scaffold. For each organelle, learn what it does, how proteins reach it, and which disease follows when it fails: lysosomal storage, peroxisomal, mitochondrial and ciliary disorders all make sense once the normal pathway is clear.
objectives: Explain how a secretory or lysosomal protein travels from the ribosome to its destination.
Distinguish the functions of rough ER, smooth ER, Golgi, lysosomes, peroxisomes and mitochondria.
Explain why I-cell disease raises plasma lysosomal enzyme levels.
Distinguish the three cytoskeletal filament classes and their motor proteins.
Apply organelle biology to explain primary ciliary dyskinesia and mitochondrial disease.

sections.body:
- Nucleus: double envelope continuous with the rough ER, crossed by nuclear pore complexes. The nucleolus makes rRNA and assembles ribosomal subunits. Lamins (intermediate filaments) line the inner envelope.
- Ribosomes: eukaryotic 80S (60S + 40S); bacterial 70S (50S + 30S). Svedberg values are not additive. The difference lets some antibiotics target bacterial ribosomes selectively.
- Rough ER: ribosomes translating secretory, membrane and lysosomal proteins dock here. Folding, disulphide bonds and N-linked glycosylation begin in the lumen.
- Smooth ER: lipid and steroid synthesis, cytochrome P450 drug metabolism (plentiful in hepatocytes) and Ca²⁺ storage (the sarcoplasmic reticulum of muscle).
- Golgi apparatus: modifies and sorts proteins from its cis to its trans face, then dispatches them to the plasma membrane, secretory granules or lysosomes.
- Lysosomes: acid hydrolases working at about pH 4.5–5, kept acidic by a proton pump. They digest material from endocytosis and autophagy.
- Peroxisomes: begin oxidation of very-long-chain fatty acids, break down hydrogen peroxide with catalase, and help make plasmalogens.
- Mitochondria: two membranes, with the respiratory chain on the folded inner membrane (cristae), and their own circular DNA.

Proteins made on free ribosomes stay in the cytosol or are imported into the nucleus, mitochondria or peroxisomes. Proteins with an N-terminal signal peptide are guided by the signal recognition particle to the rough ER and threaded into it as they are made. From there vesicles carry them to the Golgi.
- Lysosomal enzymes are recognised in the Golgi by GlcNAc-1-phosphotransferase, which starts building a mannose-6-phosphate (M6P) tag. M6P receptors in the trans-Golgi network capture tagged enzymes and send them to the lysosome. Untagged proteins follow the default route out of the cell.
- The mitochondrial genome (about 16,500 base pairs) holds 37 genes: 13 encode oxidative phosphorylation proteins and the rest encode tRNAs and rRNAs. Most mitochondrial proteins are therefore nuclear-encoded and imported.

Cytoskeleton
- Actin microfilaments (about 7 nm): cell shape, microvilli, cytokinesis and, with myosin, contraction.
- Intermediate filaments (about 10 nm): tensile strength. They are tissue-specific (keratins in epithelia, vimentin in mesenchymal cells, desmin in muscle, GFAP in astrocytes), which helps pathologists type tumours.
- Microtubules (α/β-tubulin, about 25 nm): mitotic spindle, cilia and transport tracks. Kinesins generally move cargo towards the plus end and dyneins towards the minus end. Motile cilia have a 9 + 2 arrangement of microtubules, moved by dynein arms.

A 9-month-old has coarse facial features, overgrown gums, stiff joints and slow development. Her cells are full of inclusions, yet the activity of several lysosomal enzymes in her plasma is high. This is I-cell disease (mucolipidosis II, autosomal recessive, GNPTAB variants). Without the phosphotransferase, lysosomal enzymes get no M6P tag, so they are secreted instead of delivered: the plasma has too much enzyme and the lysosomes too little, and undigested material builds up.

The same reasoning explains other disorders:
- Primary ciliary dyskinesia: defective dynein arms stop cilia beating, so mucus is not cleared, giving chronic chest infection, bronchiectasis, ear infections and reduced fertility. Around 40% have situs inversus (Kartagener syndrome), because ciliary movement helps set left–right asymmetry in the embryo.
- Zellweger spectrum disorders: peroxisomes fail to form, so very-long-chain fatty acids accumulate.
- Mitochondrial DNA disease (for example MELAS or Leber hereditary optic neuropathy) is passed down the maternal line, and the proportion of mutant mtDNA in a cell (heteroplasmy) affects severity.
- Drugs: colchicine and vinca alkaloids stop microtubule assembly; taxanes stabilise microtubules. Either way the mitotic spindle cannot work.

- Students often think lysosomes start very-long-chain fatty acid oxidation. In fact peroxisomes do; mitochondria finish the job.
- Students often think every mitochondrial disease is maternally inherited. Most mitochondrial proteins are nuclear-encoded, so many mitochondrial disorders follow Mendelian patterns.
- Students often add Svedberg values (60S + 40S = 100S). Sedimentation depends on shape as well as mass, so the whole ribosome is 80S.
- Students often think a lysosomal storage disease always means low plasma enzyme. In I-cell disease plasma levels are high because the enzymes are misrouted, not missing.
- Students often call intermediate filaments 'motor tracks'. Motors run on microtubules (kinesin, dynein) and actin (myosin); intermediate filaments give mechanical strength.

notes.h: Membranes, transport and the membrane potential
notes.overview: The plasma membrane is a lipid bilayer that ions and most polar molecules cannot cross unaided. Transport proteins set up and use ion gradients, and those gradients create the resting membrane potential. Many drugs and diseases (digoxin, SGLT2 inhibitors, cystic fibrosis, hyperkalaemia) are easiest to understand as changes to these proteins or gradients.
objectives: Distinguish simple diffusion, facilitated diffusion, primary and secondary active transport, with an example of each.
Apply the Nernst equation to calculate an equilibrium potential and predict the effect of a change in plasma K⁺.
Explain why the resting membrane potential lies close to E_K.
Explain how loss of CFTR function produces thick airway secretions.
Interpret the effect of hyperkalaemia on cardiac excitability.

sections.h: Membrane structure and routes across it
sections.body:
The fluid mosaic model describes a phospholipid bilayer with hydrophobic tails inside and hydrophilic heads facing water, with proteins floating in it. Cholesterol buffers fluidity. The two leaflets differ: phosphatidylserine normally faces the cytosol and flips outwards in apoptosis as an 'eat me' signal.
- Simple diffusion: small non-polar molecules (O₂, CO₂, steroid hormones) cross down their gradient. The rate rises with area and gradient and falls with thickness (Fick's law).
- Facilitated diffusion: channels or carriers (for example GLUT transporters) move solutes down their gradient without ATP. Carriers are specific and saturable.
- Primary active transport: ATP is used directly. The Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase moves 3 Na⁺ out and 2 K⁺ in per cycle, so it is electrogenic. Other examples are Ca²⁺-ATPases and the gastric H⁺/K⁺-ATPase.
- Secondary active transport (co-transport): a gradient made by a primary pump drives another solute. Symporters move both the same way (SGLT1 in gut, SGLT2 in proximal tubule); antiporters move them in opposite directions (the Na⁺/Ca²⁺ exchanger).
- Vesicular transport: receptor-mediated endocytosis in clathrin-coated pits (for example LDL via the LDL receptor) and exocytosis.

sections.h: Equilibrium potentials and the resting potential
sections.body:
An ion's equilibrium potential is the voltage at which its electrical and concentration gradients balance. The Nernst equation gives it: E = (RT/zF) ln([out]/[in]), which at 37 °C is about (61.5/z) × log₁₀([out]/[in]) mV.
- Worked example: K⁺ 4 mM outside and 140 mM inside. log₁₀(4/140) = −1.544, so E_K ≈ 61.5 × −1.544 ≈ −95 mV.
- At rest the membrane is far more permeable to K⁺ than to other ions, so the resting potential lies close to E_K (typically about −70 to −90 mV depending on cell type; approximate). The Goldman–Hodgkin–Katz equation weights each ion by its permeability.
- The Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase adds only a few millivolts directly. Its main job is to maintain the gradients that the leak channels then use.
- If plasma K⁺ rises to 7 mM, E_K = 61.5 × log₁₀(7/140) ≈ 61.5 × −1.30 ≈ −80 mV. The resting potential moves in the same direction, so cells depolarise.

sections.h: Transport defects and the clinical picture
sections.body:
- Cystic fibrosis: CFTR is an apical chloride channel (also passing bicarbonate) opened by cAMP-dependent phosphorylation. When it fails, less chloride and water are secreted, airway surface liquid shrinks and mucus becomes thick and sticky. The commonest variant, F508del, removes one amino acid; the protein misfolds and is degraded before reaching the membrane.
- Familial hypercholesterolaemia: faulty LDL receptor endocytosis leaves LDL in the plasma.
- Hyperkalaemia: membranes depolarise. At first excitability rises, but sustained depolarisation inactivates voltage-gated Na⁺ channels, so conduction slows and severe hyperkalaemia can stop the heart.
- Drugs acting on transporters: digoxin inhibits the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase; SGLT2 inhibitors block renal glucose reabsorption; proton pump inhibitors block the gastric H⁺/K⁺-ATPase.

An older man taking digoxin is found to have a raised plasma K⁺. Why do transport principles matter here?
- Digoxin binds the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase and reduces pumping. Intracellular Na⁺ rises, so the Na⁺/Ca²⁺ exchanger removes less Ca²⁺ and cardiac contractility increases (the intended effect).
- Digoxin competes with K⁺ at the pump, so low plasma K⁺ makes its effects stronger; in toxicity, widespread pump block lets K⁺ leak out of cells and plasma K⁺ can rise.
- Separately, a high plasma K⁺ reduces the K⁺ gradient. By the Nernst equation E_K becomes less negative, the resting potential depolarises, Na⁺ channels inactivate, and conduction slows. ECG changes such as peaked T waves and a widening QRS warn of danger.
The general lesson: when a drug or disease alters a pump, channel or gradient, follow the ions step by step to predict the effect.

- Students often think the Na⁺/K⁺ pump directly creates most of the resting potential. In fact it contributes only a few millivolts directly; K⁺ leak down the gradient it maintains does most of the work.
- Students often think facilitated diffusion needs energy because it uses a protein. It does not; it only moves solute down its gradient, but it is saturable.
- Students often say secondary active transport does not use ATP. It uses ATP indirectly, through the Na⁺ gradient set up by the pump.
- Students often think hyperkalaemia simply makes the heart 'more excitable'. Mild rises can, but sustained depolarisation inactivates Na⁺ channels and reduces excitability and conduction.
- Students often think F508del is a frameshift. It is an in-frame deletion of three bases removing one phenylalanine.

notes.h: Protein structure, haemoglobin and enzyme kinetics
notes.overview: A protein's amino acid sequence decides how it folds, and its fold decides what it does. Haemoglobin shows how cooperative binding and allosteric effectors tune function. Enzyme kinetics (Km, Vmax and the types of inhibition) explains how many drugs work and why some effects outlast the drug.
objectives: Explain the four levels of protein structure and the bonds that stabilise each.
Explain why haemoglobin's oxygen dissociation curve is sigmoidal and what shifts it.

sections.body:
- Glycolysis (cytosol): glucose → 2 pyruvate, net 2 ATP and 2 NADH. Three irreversible steps are controlled: hexokinase or glucokinase, phosphofructokinase-1 (PFK-1) and pyruvate kinase.
- Without oxygen (or in red cells, which have no mitochondria), lactate dehydrogenase turns pyruvate into lactate to regenerate NAD⁺.
- Link reaction (mitochondrial matrix): pyruvate dehydrogenase (PDH) makes acetyl-CoA. It is irreversible and needs thiamine pyrophosphate, lipoate, CoA, FAD and NAD⁺.
- Krebs (TCA) cycle: each turn gives 3 NADH, 1 FADH₂, 1 GTP and 2 CO₂.
- Oxidative phosphorylation: complexes of the inner membrane pass electrons to O₂ and pump protons; ATP synthase uses the proton gradient (Mitchell's chemiosmotic theory).
- Gluconeogenesis (liver, and kidney): bypasses the irreversible steps with pyruvate carboxylase, PEP carboxykinase, fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase and glucose-6-phosphatase. Substrates are lactate (Cori cycle), alanine and glycerol.
- Pentose phosphate pathway: makes NADPH and ribose-5-phosphate; glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) is the rate-limiting step.

- PFK-1 is the main control point. AMP and fructose-2,6-bisphosphate activate it; ATP and citrate inhibit it. Insulin raises fructose-2,6-bisphosphate (favouring glycolysis); glucagon lowers it (favouring gluconeogenesis).
- Glucokinase (liver and pancreatic β-cells) has a lower affinity for glucose than hexokinase and is not inhibited by glucose-6-phosphate, so its activity tracks blood glucose. Glucokinase variants cause a form of MODY.
- Glycogen synthase is activated by insulin; glycogen phosphorylase by glucagon (liver) and adrenaline, via cAMP. Muscle has no glucose-6-phosphatase, so its glycogen fuels only the muscle.
- Even-chain fatty acids give only acetyl-CoA; PDH is irreversible and acetyl-CoA's two carbons are lost as CO₂ in the cycle, so they make no net glucose.
- Approximate ATP per glucose (P/O about 2.5 per NADH and 1.5 per FADH₂): glycolysis 2 ATP + 2 NADH (3 or 5 ATP depending on the shuttle); PDH 2 NADH (5); Krebs 6 NADH (15), 2 FADH₂ (3), 2 GTP (2). Total about 30–32 ATP.
- Inhibitors and uncouplers: cyanide and carbon monoxide block complex IV; 2,4-dinitrophenol and thermogenin (brown fat) let protons bypass ATP synthase, releasing energy as heat.

- Glycogen storage disease type I (von Gierke; glucose-6-phosphatase system, autosomal recessive): the liver cannot release free glucose, so fasting hypoglycaemia, with lactic acidosis, hyperuricaemia, hyperlipidaemia and hepatomegaly.
- McArdle disease (muscle glycogen phosphorylase): exercise intolerance and cramps, sometimes with myoglobinuria; blood glucose is normal.
- G6PD deficiency (X-linked): red cells cannot make enough NADPH to keep glutathione reduced. Infection, fava beans or drugs such as primaquine, dapsone or rasburicase trigger haemolysis, with Heinz bodies and bite cells.
- Pyruvate kinase deficiency (autosomal recessive): red cells depend on glycolysis for ATP, so a chronic haemolytic anaemia results.
- Thiamine deficiency (for example in alcohol dependence) impairs PDH and α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase, so pyruvate is diverted to lactate.

- Lactate rises whenever oxidative phosphorylation fails (shock, cyanide, carbon monoxide) or pyruvate cannot enter mitochondria.

- Fatty acid synthesis (cytosol, fed state): acetyl-CoA leaves mitochondria as citrate; acetyl-CoA carboxylase (biotin-dependent, rate-limiting) makes malonyl-CoA; fatty acid synthase uses NADPH to build palmitate.
- β-oxidation (mitochondria, fasting): long-chain fatty acids enter by the carnitine shuttle (CPT-I). Each cycle yields 1 FADH₂, 1 NADH and 1 acetyl-CoA.
- Ketogenesis (liver mitochondria): in fasting and insulin deficiency, acetyl-CoA becomes acetoacetate and β-hydroxybutyrate, a fuel for brain, heart and muscle. The liver cannot use ketones itself.
- Cholesterol synthesis: HMG-CoA reductase is rate-limiting and is the target of statins.
- Lipoproteins: chylomicrons (apoB-48) carry dietary triglyceride; VLDL (apoB-100) carries hepatic triglyceride; lipoprotein lipase, activated by apoC-II, releases their fatty acids; LDL (apoB-100) delivers cholesterol via the LDL receptor; HDL (apoA-I) returns cholesterol to the liver.
- Amino acids: transamination (ALT, AST; pyridoxal phosphate) passes amino groups to glutamate, which releases ammonia. The urea cycle in the liver turns ammonia into urea.

- Malonyl-CoA inhibits CPT-I, so newly made fatty acids are not burned straight away. In fasting, glucagon and AMP-activated kinase switch off acetyl-CoA carboxylase, malonyl-CoA falls and β-oxidation runs.

- Low cholesterol inside a liver cell increases LDL receptor numbers; statins work partly this way, so LDL clearance from plasma rises.
- Urea cycle: carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I and ornithine transcarbamylase (OTC) act in mitochondria, the rest in the cytosol. OTC combines carbamoyl phosphate with ornithine to make citrulline.
- In OTC deficiency citrulline is low, and unused carbamoyl phosphate spills into pyrimidine synthesis, so urinary orotic acid rises. Ammonia and glutamine accumulate. Ammonia stimulates breathing, so a respiratory alkalosis is typical.
- Amino acid carbon skeletons are glucogenic or ketogenic; leucine and lysine are purely ketogenic.

- Homocystinuria (cystathionine β-synthase, autosomal recessive): lens dislocation, clotting risk, tall stature and skeletal changes.

objectives: Convert a DNA coding or template strand into mRNA and an amino acid sequence.

- Primase lays down short RNA primers; DNA polymerases extend them, adding nucleotides only to a 3′ end, so new DNA is always made 5′→3′.

- Polymerases proofread, but some errors escape and must be repaired.
- Telomerase, a reverse transcriptase carrying its own RNA template, extends chromosome ends in germ cells, stem cells and most cancers.

- Mismatch repair (MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, PMS2) fixes mispaired bases and small loops after replication, especially in repetitive microsatellites.

Transcription
- RNA polymerase II makes mRNA (polymerase I makes most rRNA; III makes tRNA). Transcription factors bind promoters; enhancers act at a distance.

- The code is read in triplets from AUG (methionine); UAA, UAG and UGA are stop codons. The code is degenerate: most amino acids have more than one codon.

- Frameshift: an insertion or deletion not divisible by three shifts the reading frame, usually producing a premature stop.

- Coding strand 5′-ATG GCT TGG AAA-3′ gives mRNA 5′-AUG GCU UGG AAA-3′, read as Met–Ala–Trp–Lys.

- If TGG mutates to TGA, the mRNA codon becomes UGA, a stop codon: a nonsense mutation, so the peptide stops after Met–Ala.
- If one base is deleted from the second codon, every codon after it is read in a new frame: a frameshift.

notes.h: Cell signalling, the cell cycle and apoptosis
notes.overview: Cells respond to signals through four main receptor classes, each with its own speed and second messengers. The same switches that control signalling also control division: cyclins and CDKs drive the cycle, Rb and p53 apply the brakes, and apoptosis removes damaged cells. Cancer and several toxins make sense once these switches are clear.
objectives: Distinguish the four main receptor classes by mechanism, speed and example.
Explain the Gs, Gi and Gq pathways and how cholera and pertussis toxins disturb them.
Explain how Rb and p53 control the G1/S transition.
Distinguish the intrinsic and extrinsic pathways of apoptosis.

sections.body:
- Ligand-gated ion channels (for example nicotinic acetylcholine and GABA-A receptors): binding opens a channel; responses take milliseconds.
- G protein-coupled receptors (seven transmembrane segments): activate a heterotrimeric G protein. Gs stimulates adenylyl cyclase (cAMP rises, protein kinase A is activated); Gi inhibits adenylyl cyclase; Gq activates phospholipase C, which splits PIP₂ into IP₃ (releases Ca²⁺ from the ER) and DAG (activates protein kinase C). The signal ends when Gα hydrolyses its GTP.
- Receptor tyrosine kinases (insulin receptor, EGFR, HER2): ligand binding causes dimerisation and autophosphorylation, recruiting adaptors that switch on the Ras–MAPK and PI3K–Akt pathways. Ras is a small GTPase, active when bound to GTP.
- Cytokine receptors (for example the erythropoietin receptor) have associated JAK kinases, which phosphorylate STATs, transcription factors that then enter the nucleus.
- Intracellular receptors (steroid and thyroid hormones, vitamin D): the hormone crosses the membrane, and the receptor acts as a transcription factor. Effects are slow in onset and long-lasting.

The cycle runs G1 → S (DNA synthesis) → G2 → M (mitosis and cytokinesis); G0 is a resting state outside the cycle.
- Cyclins activate cyclin-dependent kinases (CDKs). At the restriction point in G1, cyclin D–CDK4/6 (then cyclin E–CDK2) phosphorylates Rb. Unphosphorylated Rb holds the E2F transcription factors; phosphorylation releases them and S-phase genes are switched on.
- Checkpoints at G1/S and G2/M detect DNA damage; the spindle assembly checkpoint stops anaphase until all chromosomes are attached.
- DNA damage stabilises p53, which switches on p21, a CDK inhibitor, so the cell arrests to allow repair. If damage is severe, p53 promotes apoptosis. MDM2 normally keeps p53 low.
Apoptosis
- Intrinsic pathway: cell stress or DNA damage tips the BCL-2 family balance; BAX and BAK make the outer mitochondrial membrane leaky, cytochrome c is released, the apoptosome forms and caspase-9 is activated. BCL-2 itself opposes this.
- Extrinsic pathway: Fas ligand or TNF binds a death receptor, activating caspase-8.
- Both activate executioner caspases (3, 6 and 7). The cell shrinks and breaks into membrane-bound fragments, so there is little inflammation.

sections.h: Toxins and cancer: what goes wrong
sections.body:

- Pertussis toxin modifies Gi so it cannot be activated; the brake on adenylyl cyclase is lost.
- Oncogenes act dominantly: one activated allele is enough (for example mutant Ras stuck in the GTP-bound state, HER2 amplification, the BCR-ABL fusion kinase).
- Tumour suppressors need both alleles inactivated: Knudson's two-hit hypothesis, from retinoblastoma. In inherited retinoblastoma the first hit is in the germline, so tumours are earlier and often bilateral.
- Loss of p53 lets damaged cells keep dividing; JAK2 V617F drives most cases of polycythaemia vera.
- Targeted drugs follow from the biology: imatinib (BCR-ABL), trastuzumab (HER2) and CDK4/6 inhibitors.

An aid worker returning from a cholera outbreak passes many litres of pale, painless 'rice-water' stool within a day and becomes tachycardic and hypotensive.

- Losses of bicarbonate and potassium in the stool explain the metabolic acidosis and hypokalaemia.

notes.h: Patterns of inheritance and medical genetics
notes.overview: Recognising an inheritance pattern from a family tree, and turning it into a risk figure, is a core skill for the MLA's 'genetics and genomics' area. Learn the classic Mendelian patterns, the exceptions (imprinting, repeat expansions, mitochondrial inheritance, mosaicism), Hardy–Weinberg calculations, and how UK newborn screening and cascade testing put them into practice.
objectives: Interpret a pedigree to decide the most likely mode of inheritance.
Calculate carrier and recurrence risks, including the 2/3 carrier risk for an unaffected sibling.
Apply the Hardy–Weinberg equation to estimate carrier frequency from disease incidence.
Explain imprinting, anticipation and heteroplasmy with clinical examples.
Describe what the NHS newborn blood spot test screens for and why.

sections.body:
- Autosomal dominant: one altered copy is enough; affected people in successive generations; each child of an affected parent has a 1 in 2 chance; males and females equally affected, with male-to-male transmission possible. Penetrance may be incomplete and expressivity variable. Examples: Huntington disease, Marfan syndrome, familial hypercholesterolaemia, Lynch syndrome.
- Autosomal recessive: two altered copies needed; parents are usually unaffected carriers; when both parents are carriers each pregnancy has a 1 in 4 chance of an affected child; more common with consanguinity. Examples: cystic fibrosis, sickle cell disease, PKU, most inborn errors of metabolism.
- X-linked recessive: mostly males affected; no male-to-male transmission; all daughters of an affected man are carriers; a carrier woman's sons each have a 1 in 2 chance of being affected. Examples: Duchenne muscular dystrophy, haemophilia, G6PD deficiency, OTC deficiency.
- X-linked dominant: an affected father passes it to all his daughters and none of his sons.
- Mitochondrial: passed down the maternal line, because the embryo's mitochondria come from the egg; both sexes affected. Example: Leber hereditary optic neuropathy.

- Imprinting: some genes are expressed only from one parent's copy. At 15q11–q13, loss of the paternal contribution (paternal deletion in about 60%, maternal uniparental disomy in about 30%) causes Prader–Willi syndrome; loss of the maternal contribution causes Angelman syndrome.
- Repeat expansions and anticipation: an unstable repeat can grow between generations, giving earlier or more severe disease. In Huntington disease, 10–35 CAG repeats are typical, 36–39 may or may not cause disease, and 40 or more almost always do; juvenile cases usually have more than 60.
- Heteroplasmy: cells carry a mix of normal and mutant mtDNA, and the proportion affects severity.
- Mosaicism, including gonadal mosaicism, explains recurrence after an apparently new mutation.
- Lyonisation: random X-inactivation means some female carriers of X-linked conditions show signs, for example DMD carriers with cardiomyopathy.
Hardy–Weinberg: for two alleles with frequencies p and q (p + q = 1), genotype frequencies are p², 2pq and q². It assumes a large, randomly mating population with no selection, mutation or migration. For a recessive disease affecting 1 in 3,600 births, q = 1/60 and carrier frequency 2pq ≈ 2 × 1/60 ≈ 1 in 30.

- Karyotype: whole chromosomes and large rearrangements (for example trisomy 21).
- Chromosomal microarray: smaller gains and losses of DNA (copy-number variants) that a karyotype misses, though not balanced translocations.
- Targeted tests: a known family variant, or a panel of genes for a condition.
- Genome sequencing: offered for selected indications through the NHS Genomic Medicine Service in England.
- Biochemical tests can point to a genetic cause: very high creatine kinase in a boy with weakness suggests a dystrophinopathy; a sweat test supports cystic fibrosis.
- Predictive testing in an unaffected relative (for example for Huntington disease) needs careful genetic counselling first.

- The NHS newborn blood spot test, usually taken on day 5 (day of birth = day 0), screens babies in England for 10 conditions: sickle cell disease, cystic fibrosis, congenital hypothyroidism, and seven inherited metabolic diseases (PKU, MCAD deficiency, maple syrup urine disease, isovaleric acidaemia, glutaric aciduria type 1, homocystinuria and tyrosinaemia type 1). Cystic fibrosis screening is not done after 8 weeks of age because it becomes unreliable.
- Screening finds conditions where early treatment changes outcomes, such as a low-phenylalanine diet in PKU or avoiding fasting in MCAD deficiency.
- Cascade testing traces relatives of an affected person once a family variant is known; NICE recommends it for familial hypercholesterolaemia (first-, second- and when possible third-degree relatives) and for families with Lynch syndrome.
- The GMC's MLA content map lists genetics and genomics as an area of professional knowledge and 'family history of possible genetic disorder' as a presentation.

A couple's first child has cystic fibrosis. Their 25-year-old unaffected daughter asks her chance of being a carrier, and the risk to her own children.
- Both parents must be carriers (Aa × Aa), giving AA, Aa, aA and aa in equal proportions.
- The daughter is unaffected, so aa is excluded. Of the three remaining equally likely genotypes, two are carriers: her carrier risk is 2/3.
- Suppose carrier frequency in her partner's population is 1 in 25. The risk her first child is affected is 2/3 × 1/25 × 1/4 = 2/300 = 1/150.
- Carrier testing for her and her partner would replace these estimates with near-certain figures.
The same reasoning applies to other recessive conditions. For X-linked recessive conditions the key questions are whether the mother is a carrier (affected brother, raised CK in DMD carriers) and the sex of the child.

- Students often say an unaffected sibling of a child with a recessive disease has a 1/2 carrier risk. It is 2/3, because the affected genotype is excluded.
- Students often confuse penetrance and expressivity. Penetrance is whether a genotype shows any phenotype at all; expressivity is how severe it is.
- Students often think male-to-male transmission is possible in X-linked conditions. A father passes his Y, not his X, to his sons.
- Students often think every mitochondrial disease is maternally inherited. Many are caused by nuclear genes and follow Mendelian patterns.
- Students often think a negative family history excludes a genetic disorder. New mutations, incomplete penetrance, recessive inheritance and gonadal mosaicism all explain a 'sporadic' case.

- The NHS newborn blood spot test, usually taken on day 5 (day of birth = day 0), screens babies in England for 10 conditions: sickle cell disease, cystic fibrosis, congenital hypothyroidism, and seven inherited metabolic diseases (PKU, MCAD deficiency, maple syrup urine disease, isovaleric acidaemia, glutaric aciduria type 1, homocystinuria and tyrosinaemia type 1). Cystic fibrosis screening is not done after 8 weeks of age because it becomes unreliable.
- Screening finds conditions where early treatment changes outcomes, such as a low-phenylalanine diet in PKU or avoiding fasting in MCAD deficiency.
- Cascade testing traces relatives of an affected person once a family variant is known; NICE recommends it for familial hypercholesterolaemia (first-, second- and when possible third-degree relatives) and for families with Lynch syndrome.
- The GMC's MLA content map lists genetics and genomics as an area of professional knowledge and 'family history of possible genetic disorder' as a presentation.

Clinical application
A couple's first child has cystic fibrosis. Their 25-year-old unaffected daughter asks her chance of being a carrier, and the risk to her own children.
- Both parents must be carriers (Aa × Aa), giving AA, Aa, aA and aa in equal proportions.
- The daughter is unaffected, so aa is excluded. Of the three remaining equally likely genotypes, two are carriers: her carrier risk is 2/3.
- Suppose carrier frequency in her partner's population is 1 in 25. The risk her first child is affected is 2/3 × 1/25 × 1/4 = 2/300 = 1/150.
- Carrier testing for her and her partner would replace these estimates with near-certain figures.
The same reasoning applies to other recessive conditions. For X-linked recessive conditions the key questions are whether the mother is a carrier (affected brother, raised CK in DMD carriers) and the sex of the child.

Common misconceptions
- Students often say an unaffected sibling of a child with a recessive disease has a 1/2 carrier risk. It is 2/3, because the affected genotype is excluded.
- Students often confuse penetrance and expressivity. Penetrance is whether a genotype shows any phenotype at all; expressivity is how severe it is.
- Students often think male-to-male transmission is possible in X-linked conditions. A father passes his Y, not his X, to his sons.
- Students often think every mitochondrial disease is maternally inherited. Many are caused by nuclear genes and follow Mendelian patterns.
- Students often think a negative family history excludes a genetic disorder. New mutations, incomplete penetrance, recessive inheritance and gonadal mosaicism all explain a 'sporadic' case.

cards.f: What tag targets newly made hydrolases to the lysosome?
cards.b: Mannose-6-phosphate, built in the Golgi starting with GlcNAc-1-phosphotransferase; M6P receptors in the trans-Golgi network then sort tagged enzymes to lysosomes.
cards.ex: No tag means the enzyme follows the default secretory route out of the cell.

cards.f: Why is plasma lysosomal enzyme activity high in I-cell disease?
cards.b: Without GlcNAc-1-phosphotransferase the enzymes get no M6P tag, so they are secreted instead of delivered to lysosomes. Plasma has too much; lysosomes too little.
cards.ex: The enzymes are made normally but misrouted, not missing.

cards.f: Peroxisome versus lysosome: which begins very-long-chain fatty acid oxidation?
cards.b: The peroxisome. Lysosomes hold acid hydrolases for breaking down macromolecules; peroxisomes shorten very-long-chain fatty acids and break down H₂O₂ with catalase.
cards.ex: Zellweger spectrum (no peroxisomes) causes very-long-chain fatty acid build-up.

cards.f: Why are hepatocytes rich in smooth ER?
cards.b: Smooth ER holds cytochrome P450 enzymes for drug and toxin metabolism, plus enzymes for lipid and steroid synthesis, all heavy hepatic tasks.
cards.ex: Rough ER is for protein synthesis; smooth ER for lipids, P450 and Ca²⁺ storage.

cards.f: How does a secretory protein enter the rough ER?
cards.b: An N-terminal signal peptide is bound by the signal recognition particle, which brings the translating ribosome to the ER; the chain is threaded into the lumen as it is made.
cards.ex: Proteins without a signal peptide are finished on free ribosomes in the cytosol.

cards.f: Why does primary ciliary dyskinesia cause bronchiectasis and situs inversus?
cards.b: Faulty dynein arms stop cilia beating, so mucus is not cleared and infections recur. Ciliary movement in the embryo helps set left–right asymmetry, so around 40% have situs inversus.
cards.ex: One defect (dynein) explains both chest and laterality features.

cards.f: Taxanes versus vinca alkaloids: how do they affect microtubules?
cards.b: Vinca alkaloids (like colchicine) block tubulin polymerisation; taxanes stabilise microtubules so they cannot depolymerise. Both stop the mitotic spindle working.
cards.ex: Opposite effects on the polymer, same result: mitotic arrest.

cards.f: A tumour stains strongly for desmin but not keratin. What tissue of origin does this suggest?
cards.b: Muscle. Intermediate filaments are tissue-specific: keratins mark epithelium, desmin muscle, vimentin mesenchyme, GFAP astrocytes.
cards.ex: Immunohistochemistry for intermediate filaments helps identify a tumour's origin.

cards.f: Why can a mitochondrial disease be inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern?
cards.b: mtDNA encodes only 13 proteins; most mitochondrial proteins are nuclear-encoded and imported, so variants in nuclear genes follow Mendelian inheritance.
cards.ex: Maternal inheritance applies only to variants in mtDNA itself.

cards.f: Two siblings with the same mtDNA variant have very different severity. What explains this?
cards.b: Heteroplasmy: cells hold a mix of mutant and normal mtDNA, and the proportion differs between people and tissues, so severity varies.
cards.ex: The mutant load passed through the egg is variable.

cards.f: Name the motor protein that moves cargo towards the minus end of microtubules.
cards.b: Dynein (kinesins generally move towards the plus end). Axonemal dynein arms also power ciliary beating.
cards.ex: Minus end is near the centrosome or cell body; dynein carries cargo inward.

cards.f: State the stoichiometry of the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase.
cards.b: Per cycle (one ATP) it moves 3 Na⁺ out and 2 K⁺ in. The net outward movement of positive charge makes it electrogenic.
cards.ex: Three out, two in: one net positive charge leaves per cycle.

cards.f: Primary versus secondary active transport
cards.b: Primary hydrolyses ATP directly (Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase). Secondary uses a gradient made by a primary pump, e.g. SGLT2 couples glucose uptake to Na⁺ entry.
cards.ex: Both move solute uphill; only primary uses ATP itself.

cards.f: Facilitated versus simple diffusion
cards.b: Both run down the gradient without ATP, but facilitated diffusion uses a channel or carrier, so it is specific, saturable (shows a maximum rate) and can be inhibited.
cards.ex: Saturation is the clue that a carrier is involved.

cards.f: Why does the resting membrane potential lie close to E_K?
cards.b: At rest the membrane is much more permeable to K⁺ than to Na⁺ or Cl⁻, so K⁺ dominates the weighted (Goldman) average.
cards.ex: The ion with the highest permeability pulls the membrane towards its own equilibrium potential.

cards.f: Plasma K⁺ rises from 4 to 7 mM (intracellular 140 mM). What happens to E_K?
cards.b: It becomes less negative: about −95 mV to about −80 mV (61.5 × log₁₀(7/140)). Cells depolarise.
cards.ex: A smaller [out]/[in] ratio means a smaller (less negative) log term.

cards.f: Why can severe hyperkalaemia reduce cardiac excitability?
cards.b: Sustained depolarisation inactivates voltage-gated Na⁺ channels. Fewer are available to open, so the upstroke and conduction slow, the QRS widens and the heart can stop.
cards.ex: Inactivated Na⁺ channels need a negative potential to reset.

cards.f: Why does loss of CFTR function thicken airway mucus?
cards.b: Less chloride (and bicarbonate) is secreted, so less water follows; the airway surface liquid shrinks and mucus becomes thick and sticky, impairing clearance.
cards.ex: Water follows salt: no chloride secretion, no water.

cards.f: Why does F508del CFTR fail to reach the membrane?
cards.b: Deleting phenylalanine 508 makes the protein misfold; ER quality control sends it for degradation, so little reaches the apical membrane.
cards.ex: A processing (trafficking) defect, not a frameshift.

cards.f: How does inhibiting the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase increase cardiac contractility?
cards.b: Intracellular Na⁺ rises, so the Na⁺/Ca²⁺ exchanger removes less Ca²⁺; more Ca²⁺ is stored and released, strengthening contraction.
cards.ex: The Na⁺ gradient powers Ca²⁺ removal; weaken one, keep more of the other.

cards.f: How does LDL enter cells?
cards.b: By receptor-mediated endocytosis: LDL binds LDL receptors that cluster in clathrin-coated pits, which bud inwards as vesicles. Faulty receptors cause familial hypercholesterolaemia.
cards.ex: Specific receptor, coated pit, vesicle.

cards.f: Define Km.
cards.b: The substrate concentration at which the reaction rate is half Vmax. A low Km suggests high apparent affinity of the enzyme for its substrate.
cards.ex: Read it off the curve at Vmax/2.

cards.f: Competitive versus non-competitive inhibition: effects on Km and Vmax
cards.b: Competitive: apparent Km up, Vmax unchanged (overcome by more substrate). Non-competitive: Vmax down, Km unchanged (cannot be overcome).
cards.ex: Competitors fight for the active site; extra substrate wins.

cards.f: Why is haemoglobin's O₂ dissociation curve sigmoidal?
cards.b: It has four haem sites that bind cooperatively: each O₂ bound makes the next bind more readily, so saturation rises steeply over a narrow PO₂ range.
cards.ex: Myoglobin has one site, so its curve is hyperbolic.

cards.f: Why does fetal haemoglobin take O₂ from maternal blood?
cards.b: HbF binds 2,3-BPG poorly, so its affinity for O₂ is higher (curve to the left) than adult haemoglobin's at the same PO₂.
cards.ex: Less 2,3-BPG binding = higher affinity = left shift.

cards.f: In exercising muscle, which changes shift the O₂ dissociation curve, and in which direction?
cards.b: Raised CO₂, H⁺ and temperature (and 2,3-BPG) shift it right, lowering affinity so more O₂ is released to the working muscle.
cards.ex: A right shift helps unloading where demand is high.

cards.f: Why does aspirin's antiplatelet effect last days after the drug is cleared?
cards.b: It irreversibly acetylates cyclo-oxygenase, and platelets lack a nucleus so cannot make new enzyme; the effect lasts for the platelet's lifespan.
cards.ex: Irreversible inhibition is reversed only by new enzyme synthesis.

cards.f: Km 2 mM, Vmax 100 µmol/min. What is v at [S] = 2 mM and at 6 mM?
cards.b: At 2 mM: 100 × 2/4 = 50 µmol/min. At 6 mM: 100 × 6/8 = 75 µmol/min. Tripling [S] raises v by only half because the enzyme nears saturation.
cards.ex: v = Vmax[S]/(Km + [S]).

cards.f: After a house fire a patient has PaO₂ 13 kPa and SpO₂ 98% but is confused with a lactic acidosis. Why might the readings mislead?
cards.b: Carbon monoxide binds haem tightly: PaO₂ measures dissolved O₂ only, and standard oximeters read carboxyhaemoglobin as oxyhaemoglobin. Measure COHb by co-oximetry.
cards.ex: Normal PaO₂ does not mean normal O₂ content or delivery.

cards.f: Secondary versus tertiary protein structure
cards.b: Secondary: local α-helices and β-sheets held by backbone hydrogen bonds. Tertiary: whole 3D fold held by side-chain interactions (hydrophobic, ionic, hydrogen and disulphide bonds).
cards.ex: Backbone bonds (secondary) versus side-chain bonds (tertiary).

cards.f: On a Lineweaver–Burk plot, lines with and without an inhibitor cross on the y-axis. What type of inhibitor is it?
cards.b: Competitive: the y-intercept (1/Vmax) is unchanged, so Vmax is unchanged; the slope and apparent Km increase.
cards.ex: Same y-intercept = same Vmax.

cards.f: Which enzyme is the main control point of glycolysis, and what regulates it?
cards.b: Phosphofructokinase-1. AMP and fructose-2,6-bisphosphate activate it; ATP and citrate inhibit it.
cards.ex: The committed step of glycolysis senses energy charge.

cards.f: Why is glucokinase suited to liver and pancreatic β-cells?
cards.b: It has a lower affinity for glucose and is not inhibited by glucose-6-phosphate, so its activity rises with blood glucose across the physiological range: a glucose sensor.
cards.ex: Hexokinase is saturated at normal glucose; glucokinase is not.

cards.f: Why can muscle glycogen not raise blood glucose?
cards.b: Muscle lacks glucose-6-phosphatase, so glucose-6-phosphate from glycogen cannot leave as free glucose; it is used within the muscle.
cards.ex: Only liver (and kidney) can export glucose.

cards.f: Why can even-chain fatty acids not make net glucose?
cards.b: They yield only acetyl-CoA. PDH is irreversible and the two acetyl carbons are lost as CO₂ in the Krebs cycle, so no net oxaloacetate is made.
cards.ex: Glycerol from triglyceride can make glucose; the fatty acid chains cannot.

cards.f: A toddler has fasting hypoglycaemia with high lactate, high urate, hyperlipidaemia and a big liver. Which enzyme system is likely deficient?
cards.b: Glucose-6-phosphatase (glycogen storage disease type I, von Gierke). The liver cannot release free glucose; glucose-6-phosphate is diverted to lactate, urate and lipid.
cards.ex: Hypoglycaemia plus lactic acidosis plus hepatomegaly suggests GSD I.

cards.f: Why does G6PD deficiency cause haemolysis under oxidant stress?
cards.b: Red cells rely on the pentose phosphate pathway for NADPH to keep glutathione reduced. Without it, oxidants denature haemoglobin (Heinz bodies) and damage membranes.
cards.ex: No mitochondria, so red cells depend on this pathway for NADPH.

cards.f: Von Gierke versus McArdle disease
cards.b: Von Gierke (liver glucose-6-phosphatase): fasting hypoglycaemia, lactic acidosis, hepatomegaly. McArdle (muscle phosphorylase): exercise cramps and myoglobinuria with normal blood glucose.
cards.ex: Liver glycogen serves the blood; muscle glycogen serves the muscle.

cards.f: How many ATP come from one glucose fully oxidised (P/O 2.5 and 1.5)?
cards.b: About 30–32: glycolysis 2 + shuttle 3 or 5, PDH 5, Krebs 15 (NADH) + 3 (FADH₂) + 2 (GTP).
cards.ex: The range depends on which shuttle carries cytosolic NADH into mitochondria.

cards.f: How do uncouplers such as 2,4-dinitrophenol cause hyperthermia?
cards.b: They let protons cross the inner mitochondrial membrane without passing ATP synthase. Electron transport speeds up but the energy is released as heat rather than ATP.
cards.ex: Thermogenin does this physiologically in brown fat.

cards.f: Why can a G6PD assay be normal during an acute haemolytic episode?
cards.b: The oldest, most deficient red cells have been destroyed, and the young cells and reticulocytes that remain have more enzyme. Repeat after recovery.
cards.ex: Test timing matters for red cell enzyme assays.

cards.f: How does malonyl-CoA stop fatty acid synthesis and oxidation running at the same time?
cards.b: Malonyl-CoA, made by acetyl-CoA carboxylase in the fed state, inhibits CPT-I, so fatty acids cannot enter mitochondria for β-oxidation while synthesis is active.
cards.ex: One molecule links the two pathways reciprocally.

cards.f: Why does MCAD deficiency cause hypoketotic hypoglycaemia?
cards.b: Fatty acids cannot be fully oxidised, so the liver makes too few ketones and lacks the energy and acetyl-CoA that support gluconeogenesis; glucose falls without a matching ketone rise.
cards.ex: Fasting fuel switch fails: no fat-derived fuel, so glucose is used up.

cards.f: Why can the liver not use ketone bodies?
cards.b: It lacks succinyl-CoA:3-ketoacid CoA transferase, the enzyme that activates acetoacetate, so ketones are exported to other tissues.
cards.ex: Producer, not consumer.

cards.f: A neonate has very high ammonia, low citrulline and high urinary orotic acid. Which enzyme is likely deficient?
cards.b: Ornithine transcarbamylase. Carbamoyl phosphate cannot form citrulline, so it spills into pyrimidine synthesis (orotic acid).
cards.ex: In CPS-I deficiency orotic acid is not raised.

cards.f: Why does hyperammonaemia cause a respiratory alkalosis?
cards.b: Ammonia stimulates the respiratory centre, causing hyperventilation, so PaCO₂ falls and pH rises.
cards.ex: A sick neonate with respiratory alkalosis and no lung disease: check ammonia.

cards.f: Which apolipoprotein activates lipoprotein lipase?
cards.b: ApoC-II. Lipoprotein lipase then releases fatty acids from chylomicron and VLDL triglyceride.
cards.ex: Deficiency of either causes very high triglycerides.

cards.f: How do statins lower plasma LDL cholesterol?
cards.b: They inhibit HMG-CoA reductase; lower liver cell cholesterol increases LDL receptor numbers, so more LDL is cleared from the blood.
cards.ex: Most of the effect is via increased LDL receptor clearance.

cards.f: Under NICE CG71, which relatives should cascade testing reach once FH is confirmed in someone?
cards.b: At least first- and second-degree relatives, and third-degree when possible; once the family variant is known, test for it rather than relying on LDL cholesterol.
cards.ex: Autosomal dominant: half of first-degree relatives are expected to be affected.

cards.f: Homocystinuria versus Marfan syndrome
cards.b: Both give tall stature and lens dislocation, but homocystinuria (CBS deficiency, recessive) adds clotting risk and is metabolic; Marfan (fibrillin-1, dominant) is a connective tissue disorder.
cards.ex: Thrombosis plus lens dislocation suggests homocystinuria.

cards.f: How is MCAD deficiency detected in UK newborns?
cards.b: On the newborn blood spot test (usually day 5), by measuring acylcarnitines, especially raised octanoylcarnitine (C8).
cards.ex: Early detection allows fasting to be avoided.

cards.f: Coding strand 5′-ATG CCT AAA-3′. Give the mRNA and peptide.
cards.b: mRNA 5′-AUG CCU AAA-3′ (same as coding strand, U for T); peptide Met–Pro–Lys.
cards.ex: The coding strand and mRNA have the same sequence apart from T/U.

cards.f: Why is the lagging strand made in fragments?
cards.b: Polymerases only extend a 3′ end (5′→3′ synthesis). The lagging template runs the other way, so it is copied in short Okazaki fragments that ligase joins.
cards.ex: Antiparallel strands plus one-direction polymerase = one discontinuous strand.

cards.f: Nonsense versus frameshift mutation
cards.b: Nonsense: one base change creates a premature stop codon. Frameshift: an insertion or deletion not divisible by three shifts the reading frame, usually leading to a premature stop.
cards.ex: Ask: did the frame move, or did one codon become stop?

cards.f: Which repair pathway is defective in Lynch syndrome?
cards.b: Mismatch repair (MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, PMS2; EPCAM deletions silence MSH2), giving microsatellite instability and early colorectal, endometrial and other cancers.
cards.ex: Mismatch repair catches errors at repetitive microsatellites.

cards.f: Which repair pathway is defective in xeroderma pigmentosum?
cards.b: Nucleotide excision repair, which removes UV-induced pyrimidine dimers; patients have extreme sun sensitivity and a very high skin cancer risk.
cards.ex: Bulky UV lesions need excision of a whole stretch of nucleotides.

cards.f: Why do in-frame DMD deletions usually cause Becker rather than Duchenne?
cards.b: The reading frame is kept, so a shorter but partly functional dystrophin is made; frame-shifting deletions give premature stops and no functional dystrophin (Duchenne).
cards.ex: Severity follows the reading frame more than deletion size.

cards.f: A colorectal tumour has lost MLH1 and PMS2 staining and carries BRAF V600E. What does this suggest?
cards.b: A sporadic MMR-deficient tumour, usually from MLH1 promoter hypermethylation, rather than Lynch syndrome; BRAF V600E argues against a germline cause.
cards.ex: MLH1 loss needs BRAF/methylation testing before germline testing.

cards.f: A tumour has lost MSH2 and MSH6 staining. What does NICE advise next?
cards.b: Offer germline testing for Lynch syndrome. MSH2 loss is not explained by MLH1 methylation, and MSH6 is lost with it because the partners are unstable alone.
cards.ex: Only abnormal MLH1 goes through BRAF and methylation testing first.

cards.f: Why can aminoglycosides target bacteria without blocking human protein synthesis?
cards.b: They act on the bacterial 30S subunit of the 70S ribosome, which differs from the human 80S ribosome's 40S and 60S subunits.
cards.ex: Selective toxicity exploits structural differences.

cards.f: Why can a single base change at an intron–exon boundary cause disease without altering any codon?
cards.b: It can disrupt the splice site, so the spliceosome skips an exon or keeps part of an intron; the mRNA then encodes an abnormal or truncated protein (common in β-thalassaemia).
cards.ex: Splicing signals are part of the gene even though they are not codons.

cards.f: Describe the Gq pathway.
cards.b: Gq activates phospholipase C, which splits PIP₂ into IP₃ and DAG. IP₃ releases Ca²⁺ from the ER; DAG with Ca²⁺ activates protein kinase C.
cards.ex: Two messengers from one lipid.

cards.f: Why does cholera cause profuse watery diarrhoea?
cards.b: Toxin locks Gsα active, so adenylyl cyclase stays on and cAMP stays high; protein kinase A opens CFTR and chloride and water are secreted into the gut lumen.
cards.ex: A switch stuck on, not tissue destruction.

cards.f: Why does oral rehydration solution work in cholera?
cards.b: Glucose–sodium co-transport (SGLT1) is intact; absorbing glucose with sodium drags water back into the body despite ongoing secretion.
cards.ex: The toxin spares the absorptive co-transporter.

cards.f: Cholera toxin versus pertussis toxin
cards.b: Cholera modifies Gsα so it stays active (stimulator stuck on). Pertussis modifies Gi so it cannot be activated (inhibitor switched off). Both raise cAMP.
cards.ex: Same result, opposite targets.

cards.f: What does Rb do at the G1/S restriction point?
cards.b: Unphosphorylated Rb binds E2F and blocks S-phase genes. Cyclin D–CDK4/6 then cyclin E–CDK2 phosphorylate Rb, releasing E2F so the cell enters S phase.
cards.ex: Phosphorylated Rb is inactive.

cards.f: How does p53 arrest the cell cycle after DNA damage?
cards.b: Damage stabilises p53, which switches on p21, a CDK inhibitor; Rb stays unphosphorylated and the cell pauses at G1/S to repair, or undergoes apoptosis if damage is severe.
cards.ex: MDM2 normally keeps p53 low.

cards.f: Intrinsic versus extrinsic apoptosis
cards.b: Intrinsic: stress tips the BCL-2 balance, BAX/BAK release cytochrome c, caspase-9. Extrinsic: Fas ligand or TNF binds a death receptor, caspase-8. Both activate caspases 3, 6 and 7.
cards.ex: Mitochondria for intrinsic, death receptors for extrinsic.

cards.f: A child develops retinoblastoma in both eyes at 1 year. What does Knudson's hypothesis predict about inheritance?
cards.b: Likely a germline RB1 variant (first hit in every cell), so only one somatic hit is needed per tumour: earlier, bilateral and multiple tumours; offspring have about a 1 in 2 chance of inheriting it.
cards.ex: Hereditary cases need one more hit; sporadic cases need two.

cards.f: Oncogene versus tumour suppressor gene
cards.b: Oncogene: gain of function, one mutant allele enough (dominant at cell level), e.g. Ras. Tumour suppressor: loss of function, both alleles must be lost, e.g. RB1, TP53.
cards.ex: Accelerator stuck on versus brakes removed.

cards.f: Which receptor class do steroid and thyroid hormones use, and how fast is the response?
cards.b: Intracellular receptors that act as transcription factors; effects take hours to days and last a long time.
cards.ex: Changing gene expression takes time.

cards.f: Unaffected sibling of a child with an autosomal recessive disease: carrier risk?
cards.b: 2/3. With both parents carriers, the sibling is not aa, so of AA, Aa and aA, two of three are carriers.
cards.ex: Remove the affected genotype before counting.

cards.f: Penetrance versus expressivity
cards.b: Penetrance: the proportion of people with a genotype who show any phenotype. Expressivity: the range of severity among those who do.
cards.ex: Whether versus how much.

cards.f: A pedigree shows an affected father with an affected son. Which pattern does this rule out?
cards.b: X-linked inheritance (dominant or recessive), because a father passes his Y chromosome, not his X, to his sons.
cards.ex: Male-to-male transmission excludes X-linkage.

cards.f: A recessive disease affects 1 in 10,000 births. Estimate the carrier frequency.
cards.b: q = √(1/10,000) = 1/100; 2pq ≈ 2 × 1/100 = 1/50. About 1 in 50 people are carriers (assuming Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium).
cards.ex: Carrier frequency ≈ 2q when q is small.

cards.f: Prader–Willi versus Angelman: genetic basis
cards.b: Both involve imprinted 15q11–q13. Loss of the paternal contribution (deletion or maternal UPD) gives Prader–Willi; loss of the maternal contribution (deletion or paternal UPD) gives Angelman.
cards.ex: Same region, opposite parent of origin.

cards.f: Why does Huntington disease show anticipation?
cards.b: The HTT CAG repeat is unstable and often expands when passed on; larger repeats are linked to earlier onset (juvenile cases usually above 60 repeats).
cards.ex: Repeat length roughly predicts age of onset.

cards.f: How can a female carrier of an X-linked recessive disorder have symptoms?
cards.b: Through skewed X-inactivation (lyonisation): if most cells silence the normal X, the variant is expressed. DMD carriers can develop cardiomyopathy.
cards.ex: X-inactivation is random cell by cell.

cards.f: Why can mitochondrial disease severity differ between siblings?
cards.b: Heteroplasmy: each egg receives a different proportion of mutant mtDNA, and tissues differ too, so severity varies.
cards.ex: Not all mitochondria in a cell carry the variant.

cards.f: How many conditions does the NHS newborn blood spot test screen for in England, and when is it usually taken?
cards.b: Ten (sickle cell disease, cystic fibrosis, congenital hypothyroidism and seven inherited metabolic diseases); usually on day 5, counting birth as day 0.
cards.ex: Early treatment changes outcomes for each listed condition.

cards.f: Mother is a confirmed carrier of DMD. What is the risk that her next son is affected?
cards.b: 1 in 2 for each son (he inherits either her normal or her variant X). For a pregnancy of unknown sex the risk of an affected boy is 1 in 4.
cards.ex: Sons get mother's X; daughters also get father's X.

questions.q: Which organelle is the main site where newly made secretory proteins are translocated and N-linked glycosylation begins?
questions.why: Ribosomes guided by the signal recognition particle dock on the rough ER and thread secretory proteins into its lumen as they are made; N-linked glycosylation begins there and is modified later in the Golgi.
optWhy: Smooth ER lacks ribosomes; it makes lipids and steroids, holds P450 enzymes and stores Ca²⁺.
Correct: the rough ER receives secretory proteins during translation and starts N-linked glycosylation.
The Golgi modifies and sorts glycoproteins, but glycosylation starts earlier, in the ER.
Peroxisomes import finished proteins from the cytosol and oxidise very-long-chain fatty acids; they do not handle secretory proteins.
Lysosomes receive enzymes at the end of the pathway; they do not translocate new proteins.
questions.clue: 'Translocated' and 'N-linked glycosylation begins'.
questions.concept: Route of secretory proteins: signal peptide, rough ER, Golgi.

followUp.q: A protein has no signal peptide and no other targeting sequence. Where will it most likely end up?
followUp.why: Without a signal peptide it is made on free ribosomes and stays in the cytosol. Secretion, membrane insertion and lysosomal delivery all need entry to the ER via a signal peptide first.

questions.q: A 10-month-old has coarse facial features, gum overgrowth, joint stiffness and developmental delay. Fibroblasts contain many inclusion bodies. Plasma activity of several lysosomal hydrolases is markedly raised, but activity inside fibroblasts is low. What is the most likely underlying defect?
options: Deficiency of a single lysosomal hydrolase
Absent GlcNAc-1-phosphotransferase, so no mannose-6-phosphate tag
questions.why: High plasma enzyme with low intracellular enzyme means the enzymes are made but sent the wrong way. Without GlcNAc-1-phosphotransferase they get no mannose-6-phosphate tag and are secreted: I-cell disease (mucolipidosis II).
optWhy: A single-enzyme storage disease lowers that one enzyme everywhere; it would not raise several enzymes in plasma.
Poor acidification would reduce enzyme activity inside lysosomes but would not push many enzymes into plasma.
Peroxisome biogenesis disorders (Zellweger spectrum) raise very-long-chain fatty acids, not plasma lysosomal enzymes.
Dynein arm defects cause primary ciliary dyskinesia, with chest and laterality problems, not storage inclusions.
Correct: no M6P tag, so lysosomal enzymes are secreted (high in plasma) and lysosomes fill with undigested material.
questions.clue: Plasma enzymes high but intracellular enzymes low, with inclusion bodies.
questions.concept: Mannose-6-phosphate targeting of lysosomal enzymes.

followUp.q: In a laboratory cell line the tagging enzyme works normally but the M6P receptor in the trans-Golgi network is absent. What would you expect to find?
options: Low enzyme activity in the culture medium
Raised lysosomal enzyme activity in the culture medium, with storage inclusions in the cells
followUp.why: Tagged enzymes still cannot be captured in the trans-Golgi network without the receptor, so they are secreted into the medium, and cells store undigested material: the same pattern as I-cell disease. Very-long-chain fatty acids point to peroxisomes.

questions.q: A pathologist examines a poorly differentiated tumour. It stains strongly for desmin and is negative for cytokeratin, GFAP and lymphoid markers. What is the most likely tissue of origin?
options: Smooth or skeletal muscle (a muscle sarcoma)
questions.why: Intermediate filament proteins are tissue-specific. Desmin is found in muscle cells, so a desmin-positive, keratin-negative tumour is most likely of muscle origin, such as a leiomyosarcoma or rhabdomyosarcoma.
optWhy: Carcinomas express cytokeratins, which were negative here.
Gliomas of astrocytic origin express GFAP, which was negative.
Correct: desmin is the intermediate filament of muscle.
Lymphoid markers were negative, and lymphocytes do not express desmin.
Melanomas are identified with melanocytic markers rather than desmin; it was not tested here, and desmin points elsewhere.
questions.clue: Desmin-positive, keratin- and GFAP-negative.
questions.concept: Tissue specificity of intermediate filaments.

followUp.q: A brain tumour biopsy is strongly positive for GFAP. Which cell type is it most likely derived from?
followUp.why: GFAP (glial fibrillary acidic protein) is the intermediate filament of astrocytes. Neurones contain neurofilaments, epithelia keratins and muscle desmin.

questions.q: A 30-year-old man attends a fertility clinic. He has had a wet cough and recurrent chest infections since childhood, chronic nasal congestion and repeated ear infections. A chest X-ray shows bronchiectasis and the heart on the right side. What is the most likely underlying defect?
options: Defective dynein arms in ciliary microtubules
questions.why: Chest infections from early life, bronchiectasis, upper airway disease, subfertility and situs inversus together point to primary ciliary dyskinesia with situs inversus (Kartagener syndrome). Dynein arms drive ciliary beating; without them mucus is not cleared and embryonic left–right patterning is randomised.
optWhy: Correct: dynein arm defects stop cilia beating, explaining the airway, ear, fertility and laterality features.
Cystic fibrosis also causes bronchiectasis and male infertility (absent vas deferens), but not situs inversus.
Absent peroxisomes (Zellweger spectrum) cause severe neurological disease in infancy, not this picture.
Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency causes emphysema and liver disease; it does not reverse organ position.
Mitochondrial DNA deletions affect high-energy tissues (muscle, eye, brain), not ciliary clearance or laterality.
questions.clue: Bronchiectasis plus situs inversus plus subfertility.
questions.concept: Microtubule motors (dynein) in motile cilia.

followUp.q: A child with recurrent chest infections and bronchiectasis has normal organ position. Which statement about primary ciliary dyskinesia is correct?
options: Normal organ position rules it out
It remains possible, because only a proportion of patients have situs inversus
It is excluded by a normal sweat test
followUp.why: Only around 40% of people with primary ciliary dyskinesia have situs inversus, so normal anatomy does not exclude it. A sweat test addresses cystic fibrosis, and PCD is usually autosomal recessive, occasionally X-linked.

questions.q: Describe the structure and functions of the three classes of cytoskeletal filament, naming the motor proteins that use them.
markScheme: Microfilaments: actin, about 7 nm; cell shape, microvilli, cytokinesis, contraction with myosin
Intermediate filaments: about 10 nm; tissue-specific proteins (keratins, vimentin, desmin, GFAP); tensile strength; used to type tumours
Microtubules: α/β-tubulin hollow tubes, about 25 nm; spindle, cilia (9 + 2), intracellular transport
Kinesins generally move towards the plus end, dyneins towards the minus end; myosins move on actin
A clinical link, e.g. ciliary dynein defects (PCD) or drugs acting on microtubules (colchicine, vinca alkaloids, taxanes)
questions.modelAnswer: Microfilaments are thin (about 7 nm) polymers of actin. They support cell shape and microvilli, drive cell movement and cytokinesis and, with myosin motors, cause muscle contraction. Intermediate filaments (about 10 nm) are rope-like and give tensile strength. Their proteins are tissue-specific, keratins in epithelia, vimentin in mesenchymal cells, desmin in muscle and GFAP in astrocytes, so pathologists use them to identify a tumour's origin. Microtubules are hollow tubes of α/β-tubulin about 25 nm across. They form the mitotic spindle, the 9 + 2 core of motile cilia, and tracks for transport: kinesins generally carry cargo towards the plus end and dyneins towards the minus end. Clinically, defective ciliary dynein causes primary ciliary dyskinesia, and colchicine, vinca alkaloids and taxanes act by disturbing microtubule dynamics.
questions.concept: Structure, function and motors of actin, intermediate filaments and microtubules.

questions.q: Using E = 61.5 × log₁₀([out]/[in]) mV, what is the K⁺ equilibrium potential when extracellular K⁺ is 4 mM and intracellular K⁺ is 140 mM?
questions.why: log₁₀(4/140) = log₁₀(0.0286) ≈ −1.544, and 61.5 × −1.544 ≈ −95 mV. The sign is negative because K⁺ is more concentrated inside.
optWhy: −61 mV corresponds to a tenfold gradient (log of 0.1 = −1), not a 35-fold one.
−75 mV is close to a typical resting potential, not the K⁺ equilibrium potential for these values.
+95 mV comes from inverting the ratio (in/out); K⁺ is higher inside, so E_K is negative.
Correct: 61.5 × log₁₀(4/140) ≈ −95 mV.
−154 mV is 61.5 × 2.5, which does not follow from these concentrations.
questions.clue: Concentrations given, and the simplified Nernst equation supplied.
questions.concept: Nernst equation for K⁺.

followUp.q: Extracellular Na⁺ is 145 mM and intracellular Na⁺ is 14.5 mM. What is E_Na at 37 °C?
followUp.why: 61.5 × log₁₀(145/14.5) = 61.5 × log₁₀(10) = +61.5 mV. It is positive because Na⁺ is higher outside. −61.5 mV inverts the ratio; +123 mV doubles the log term.

questions.q: A man's plasma K⁺ rises from 4 to 8 mM. Intracellular K⁺ stays at 140 mM. Using E = 61.5 × log₁₀([out]/[in]) mV, what happens to E_K and to resting cardiac myocytes?
options: E_K falls to about −110 mV and cells hyperpolarise
E_K rises to about −76 mV and cells depolarise
E_K stays at −95 mV because the pump compensates
E_K becomes positive and cells fire spontaneously
E_K rises to about −48 mV, exactly half the original value
questions.why: 61.5 × log₁₀(8/140) = 61.5 × −1.243 ≈ −76 mV, so E_K is about 19 mV less negative than at 4 mM (−95 mV). The resting potential follows E_K, so myocytes depolarise; sustained depolarisation then inactivates Na⁺ channels and slows conduction.
optWhy: Raising outside K⁺ shrinks the gradient, so E_K becomes less negative, not more.
Correct: −76 mV, a depolarising shift.
The pump cannot quickly restore a doubled plasma K⁺; E_K depends on the concentration ratio.
E_K stays negative while K⁺ is still higher inside the cell.
Halving the potential would need the log term to halve; doubling outside K⁺ changes it by only log₁₀2 (about 0.3).
questions.clue: Plasma K⁺ doubles while intracellular K⁺ is unchanged.
questions.concept: Effect of extracellular K⁺ on E_K and resting potential.

followUp.q: A patient has hypokalaemia (plasma K⁺ 2.5 mM, intracellular 140 mM). What happens to E_K?
followUp.why: 61.5 × log₁₀(2.5/140) = 61.5 × −1.748 ≈ −108 mV. A bigger gradient makes E_K more negative. −80 mV would need a higher plasma K⁺, not a lower one.

questions.q: Glucose uptake into a cell type shows a maximum rate that is not exceeded however high the glucose concentration goes. Uptake needs no ATP and stops if the gradient is reversed. Which mechanism fits best?
options: Facilitated diffusion by a GLUT carrier
questions.why: A saturable process that only runs down the gradient and needs no energy is facilitated diffusion through a carrier such as a GLUT transporter. Saturation happens because there are a limited number of carriers.
optWhy: Simple diffusion does not saturate; its rate rises in proportion to the gradient.
Primary active transport uses ATP directly and can move solute against its gradient.
Na⁺-coupled transport (SGLT) can move glucose against its gradient using the Na⁺ gradient.
Pinocytosis is non-specific vesicular uptake that uses energy and does not show this carrier-like saturation.
Correct: saturable, specific, downhill and ATP-independent is the signature of carrier-mediated facilitated diffusion.
questions.clue: Saturates, no ATP, and stops when the gradient reverses.
questions.concept: Kinetics of transport mechanisms.

followUp.q: In the proximal tubule, glucose is reabsorbed even when its concentration in the tubular cells is higher than in the filtrate. Which transporter makes this possible?
followUp.why: SGLT2 couples glucose entry to Na⁺ moving down its gradient (secondary active transport), so glucose can move uphill. GLUT2 then lets glucose leave by facilitated diffusion. Aquaporins carry water; the H⁺/K⁺-ATPase is gastric.

questions.q: A 6-year-old with cystic fibrosis is homozygous for F508del. Which statement best explains why her airway mucus is thick?
options: CFTR is made but stays permanently open, so chloride floods into the airway
A frameshift creates a premature stop codon in every allele
The CFTR protein misfolds and is degraded, so less chloride and water reach the airway surface
Goblet cells are absent from the airway
questions.why: F508del removes one phenylalanine. The protein misfolds, is retained by ER quality control and degraded, so little CFTR reaches the apical membrane. Chloride secretion falls, water does not follow, airway surface liquid shrinks and mucus becomes thick and hard to clear.
optWhy: Too much channel opening would hydrate the airway, not dry it; F508del reduces CFTR at the membrane.
F508del is an in-frame deletion of three bases; it does not shift the frame.
Correct: a misfolding (processing) defect leaves too little channel at the surface.
Goblet cells are present (often increased); the problem is the water content of the secretions.
Absent dynein arms describe primary ciliary dyskinesia, a different disease.
questions.clue: F508del homozygous; thick mucus.
questions.concept: CFTR chloride secretion and water movement.

followUp.q: A different CFTR variant reaches the membrane normally but the channel rarely opens. Which kind of drug is designed to help this defect?
options: A potentiator that increases channel opening
followUp.why: Potentiators increase the time CFTR spends open, so they suit gating defects. Correctors help misfolded protein (such as F508del) reach the membrane. The other two act on unrelated transporters.

questions.q: Explain, using the Nernst equation, why a rise in plasma K⁺ first increases cardiac excitability but at higher levels can cause conduction failure.
markScheme: E_K = 61.5 log₁₀([K⁺]out/[K⁺]in); raising [K⁺]out makes E_K less negative (e.g. 4 → 8 mM moves it from about −95 to −76 mV)
Resting potential follows E_K because resting K⁺ permeability is high, so cells depolarise towards threshold
Mild depolarisation brings cells closer to threshold, raising excitability
Sustained depolarisation inactivates voltage-gated Na⁺ channels (they need repolarisation to reset)
Fewer available Na⁺ channels slow the upstroke and conduction (wide QRS); severe cases can cause arrest
questions.modelAnswer: The Nernst equation, E_K = 61.5 log₁₀([K⁺]out/[K⁺]in) mV at body temperature, shows that the K⁺ equilibrium potential depends on the ratio of outside to inside concentration. With 140 mM inside, raising plasma K⁺ from 4 to 8 mM moves E_K from about −95 mV to about −76 mV. Because the resting membrane is mainly permeable to K⁺, the resting potential follows E_K and the cell depolarises. At first this brings it nearer threshold, so it fires more easily. But voltage-gated Na⁺ channels inactivate when the membrane stays depolarised and need a negative potential to recover. With fewer channels available, the phase 0 upstroke is smaller and slower and conduction slows, widening the QRS. At severe levels cells cannot fire properly, and dangerous arrhythmias or asystole can follow.
questions.concept: Extracellular K⁺, E_K, Na⁺ channel inactivation and excitability.

questions.q: A drug raises an enzyme's apparent Km but leaves its Vmax unchanged. Which drug–enzyme pair works this way?
questions.why: Raised apparent Km with unchanged Vmax is competitive inhibition. Methotrexate is a folate analogue that competes at the active site of dihydrofolate reductase.
optWhy: Correct: methotrexate competes with the natural substrate at the active site.
Organophosphates phosphorylate acetylcholinesterase, essentially irreversibly.
Aspirin acetylates cyclo-oxygenase irreversibly, which lowers the amount of working enzyme rather than competing reversibly.
Cyanide is usually taught as a non-competitive inhibitor of cytochrome c oxidase, lowering Vmax.
Penicillin binds its target transpeptidase irreversibly.
questions.clue: Km up, Vmax unchanged.
questions.concept: Kinetic signature of competitive inhibition.

followUp.q: An inhibitor lowers Vmax but leaves Km unchanged, and adding more substrate does not overcome it. What type of inhibition is this?
options: No inhibition: it is an assay error
followUp.why: Lower Vmax with unchanged Km is the pattern of non-competitive inhibition: the inhibitor binds away from the active site, so more substrate cannot displace it. Competitive inhibition raises Km instead.

questions.q: An enzyme has Km 2 mM and Vmax 100 µmol/min. A competitive inhibitor raises its apparent Km to 4 mM. What is the reaction rate at a substrate concentration of 6 mM with the inhibitor present?
questions.why: v = Vmax[S]/(Km + [S]) = 100 × 6/(4 + 6) = 60 µmol/min. Vmax is unchanged by a competitive inhibitor; only the apparent Km changes.
optWhy: 50 µmol/min is the rate when [S] equals Km (here it would need [S] = 4 mM).
100 µmol/min is Vmax, reached only at saturating substrate.
75 µmol/min is the rate without the inhibitor (100 × 6/8).
Correct: 100 × 6/10 = 60 µmol/min.
37.5 µmol/min halves the uninhibited rate, as if the inhibitor halved Vmax (non-competitive), which it does not.
questions.clue: Competitive inhibitor; apparent Km 4 mM; [S] 6 mM.
questions.concept: Applying Michaelis–Menten with a competitive inhibitor.

followUp.q: Same enzyme (Km 2 mM, Vmax 100 µmol/min), but now a non-competitive inhibitor halves Vmax. What is the rate at [S] = 6 mM?
followUp.why: Vmax becomes 50 and Km stays 2 mM: v = 50 × 6/8 = 37.5 µmol/min. 75 is the uninhibited rate, 60 the competitive case, and 50 is the new Vmax, not the rate at 6 mM.

questions.q: A patient taking aspirin for secondary prevention of cardiovascular disease needs elective surgery. The surgeon notes that the antiplatelet effect will persist for several days after the last tablet, even though aspirin is cleared from plasma within hours. What best explains this?
options: Aspirin is stored in fat and released slowly
Aspirin irreversibly acetylates cyclo-oxygenase, and platelets cannot make new enzyme
Aspirin competitively inhibits cyclo-oxygenase at very high affinity
Aspirin permanently damages the bone marrow megakaryocytes
Aspirin induces liver enzymes that make an active metabolite
questions.why: Aspirin covalently acetylates cyclo-oxygenase. Activity returns only when new enzyme is made, and platelets have no nucleus, so each affected platelet stays inhibited for its lifespan; recovery depends on new platelets being produced.
optWhy: Aspirin is not stored in fat; its plasma half-life is short.
Correct: irreversible acetylation plus no protein synthesis in platelets.
A competitive inhibitor's effect fades as the drug is cleared, however tight its binding.
The marrow keeps making new platelets; that is exactly how the effect wears off.
Aspirin is not a liver enzyme inducer, and this would not explain a prolonged, drug-free effect.
questions.clue: Effect lasts days although the drug is cleared within hours.
questions.concept: Irreversible inhibition and the need for new enzyme synthesis.

followUp.q: A farmer is poisoned by an organophosphate pesticide that phosphorylates acetylcholinesterase. Why can recovery of enzyme activity take a long time?
options: The enzyme is covalently modified, so activity returns mainly as new enzyme is made
The inhibition is competitive and needs high acetylcholine to overcome
Organophosphates are excreted very slowly by the kidney
Acetylcholinesterase is only made in childhood
followUp.why: Organophosphates covalently modify the active site, so recovery relies largely on synthesis of new enzyme. It is not competitive, and the enzyme is made throughout life.

questions.q: A pregnant woman's placenta transfers oxygen to the fetus efficiently even though fetal arterial PO₂ is low. Which property of fetal haemoglobin best explains this?
options: It has a right-shifted curve because it binds 2,3-BPG strongly
It is a monomer like myoglobin
It contains iron in the ferric (Fe³⁺) state
It does not show cooperative binding
It binds 2,3-BPG poorly, giving higher O₂ affinity (a left-shifted curve)
questions.why: Fetal haemoglobin (two α and two γ chains) binds 2,3-BPG less well than adult haemoglobin. With less of this right-shifting effector bound, its affinity for O₂ is higher, so at the same PO₂ in the placenta it loads O₂ from maternal haemoglobin.
optWhy: Strong 2,3-BPG binding would lower affinity, the opposite of what the fetus needs.
HbF is a tetramer, not a monomer.
Ferric (Fe³⁺) haem is methaemoglobin, which cannot carry O₂.
HbF still binds O₂ cooperatively; its curve is sigmoidal.
Correct: weak 2,3-BPG binding gives a left-shifted curve and higher affinity.
questions.clue: Efficient transfer at low fetal PO₂.
questions.concept: 2,3-BPG and haemoglobin oxygen affinity.

followUp.q: A climber spends two weeks at high altitude and red cell 2,3-BPG rises. What is the effect on the dissociation curve?
options: Shift to the left, holding O₂ more tightly
Shift to the right, releasing O₂ more readily to tissues
No change in position, only a change in shape
followUp.why: More 2,3-BPG stabilises the low-affinity form of haemoglobin, shifting the curve right and aiding unloading in tissues. Left shifts come from less 2,3-BPG, HbF or carbon monoxide.

questions.q: Explain why haemoglobin's oxygen dissociation curve is sigmoidal, why myoglobin's is hyperbolic, and why this matters for oxygen delivery.
markScheme: Haemoglobin is a tetramer with four haem sites; myoglobin is a single chain with one
Cooperative binding: O₂ binding at one subunit raises the affinity of the others (tense to relaxed state), giving a sigmoid curve
Myoglobin binds by simple equilibrium, giving a hyperbolic curve with high affinity at low PO₂
Steep part of haemoglobin's curve lies over tissue PO₂, so it loads fully in lungs and releases a large fraction in tissues; myoglobin acts as a store in muscle
questions.modelAnswer: Myoglobin is a single polypeptide with one haem, so it binds oxygen by a simple equilibrium and its curve is hyperbolic: it is nearly saturated even at low PO₂, which suits a store of oxygen in muscle. Haemoglobin has four subunits, each with a haem. When oxygen binds one subunit the tetramer shifts from a low-affinity (tense) to a high-affinity (relaxed) form, so the remaining sites bind more easily. This cooperativity makes saturation rise steeply over a narrow range of PO₂, giving a sigmoid curve. The plateau means haemoglobin is almost fully loaded at alveolar PO₂ even if that falls a little, while the steep part lies over the PO₂ found in tissues, so a small fall in PO₂ releases a lot of oxygen. Right-shifting factors (CO₂, H⁺, temperature, 2,3-BPG) increase release further in active tissues.
questions.concept: Cooperative binding and the shape of the dissociation curve.

questions.q: Which enzyme catalyses the main committed, regulated step of glycolysis?
