questions.why: PFK-1 converts fructose-6-phosphate to fructose-1,6-bisphosphate, the committed step. AMP and fructose-2,6-bisphosphate activate it; ATP and citrate inhibit it, linking glycolysis to energy charge and hormonal state.
optWhy: Hexokinase is irreversible but its product, glucose-6-phosphate, can also enter glycogen synthesis or the pentose phosphate pathway, so it is not the committed step.
Pyruvate kinase is regulated but acts at the last step, not the committed one.
Correct: PFK-1 is the main control point.
Lactate dehydrogenase is reversible and regenerates NAD⁺; it is not a control point of glycolysis.
This enzyme is a reversible step that generates NADH; it is not a major control point.
questions.clue: 'Main committed, regulated step'.
questions.concept: Regulation of glycolysis at PFK-1.

followUp.q: After a carbohydrate meal, insulin rises. How does this speed up hepatic glycolysis?
followUp.why: Insulin increases fructose-2,6-bisphosphate, a potent activator of PFK-1 (and inhibitor of fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase). Glucagon lowers it. Citrate inhibits PFK-1, and insulin increases glucokinase activity rather than inhibiting it.

questions.q: A 4-month-old has a seizure after a long gap between feeds. Blood glucose is 1.6 mmol/L, lactate is high, urate and triglycerides are raised, and the liver is large. Which enzyme system is most likely deficient?
questions.why: Fasting hypoglycaemia with lactic acidosis, hyperuricaemia, hyperlipidaemia and hepatomegaly is glycogen storage disease type I. Without the glucose-6-phosphatase system, neither glycogen breakdown nor gluconeogenesis can release free glucose, and glucose-6-phosphate is diverted to lactate, urate and lipid.
optWhy: Correct: GSD type I blocks the final step of hepatic glucose release.
MCAD deficiency causes hypoketotic hypoglycaemia in fasting, but without hepatomegaly from stored glycogen or this marked lactic acidosis.
Muscle phosphorylase deficiency (McArdle) causes exercise cramps; it does not cause hypoglycaemia or hepatomegaly.
Pyruvate kinase deficiency causes haemolytic anaemia, not fasting hypoglycaemia.
Glycogen synthase deficiency means little glycogen is stored, so the liver would not be enlarged by glycogen, and lactate is typically high after meals rather than during fasting.
questions.clue: Hypoglycaemia plus high lactate, urate and lipids, with a large liver.
questions.concept: Hepatic glucose release depends on glucose-6-phosphatase.

followUp.q: A 20-year-old gets painful cramps within minutes of intense exercise and once passed dark urine afterwards. Fasting glucose is normal. Which enzyme is most likely deficient?
followUp.why: McArdle disease (muscle phosphorylase deficiency) stops muscle using its glycogen during intense exercise, causing cramps and sometimes myoglobinuria. Blood glucose is normal because the liver is unaffected; G6PD deficiency causes haemolysis, not cramps.

questions.q: A 24-year-old man develops dark urine and jaundice three days after starting primaquine. Haemoglobin has fallen, reticulocytes are raised and the blood film shows bite cells. Which mechanism best explains this?
options: Antibodies against red cell surface antigens
A spectrin defect making red cells spherical
Loss of red cell ATP from a glycolytic enzyme defect
Failure of red cells to make NADPH, so glutathione cannot be kept reduced
Complement-mediated lysis due to absent GPI-anchored proteins
questions.why: This is oxidant-triggered haemolysis in G6PD deficiency. G6PD makes NADPH in the pentose phosphate pathway; red cells need NADPH to keep glutathione reduced. Without it, primaquine-generated oxidants denature haemoglobin into Heinz bodies, and the spleen removes them, leaving bite cells.
optWhy: Autoimmune haemolysis is antibody-mediated (positive direct antiglobulin test) and not specifically triggered by oxidant drugs with bite cells.
Hereditary spherocytosis gives spherocytes and chronic haemolysis, not acute oxidant episodes.
Pyruvate kinase deficiency lowers ATP and causes chronic haemolysis, not drug-triggered episodes with bite cells.
Correct: low G6PD means low NADPH, low reduced glutathione and oxidative damage.
Paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria involves complement and GPI anchors, not oxidant drugs.
questions.clue: Oxidant drug, bite cells, young man.
questions.concept: Pentose phosphate pathway, NADPH and glutathione in red cells.

followUp.q: A boy with known G6PD deficiency develops haemolysis during a chest infection, without any new drug. Why can infection trigger haemolysis?
options: Activated white cells release oxidants that red cells cannot neutralise
Infection lowers glucose supply to red cells
Fever activates complement on red cells
followUp.why: During infection, white cells generate reactive oxygen species, adding an oxidant load that G6PD-deficient red cells cannot neutralise without enough NADPH and reduced glutathione. The other options are not the mechanism.

questions.q: A patient is brought in after a fire in an enclosed factory. She is agitated, with a raised lactate. Blood cyanide is later found to be high. At which site does cyanide act, and why does lactate rise?
options: Complex I; NADH cannot be oxidised so glycolysis stops
Complex IV (cytochrome c oxidase); electron transfer to O₂ stops, so cells rely on anaerobic glycolysis
ATP synthase; protons leak back into the matrix
Hexokinase; glucose cannot be trapped in cells
questions.why: Cyanide blocks cytochrome c oxidase (complex IV), so electrons cannot pass to O₂ and oxidative phosphorylation stops even though O₂ is present. Cells turn to anaerobic glycolysis, regenerating NAD⁺ by making lactate, so a lactic acidosis develops.
optWhy: Rotenone, not cyanide, blocks complex I; and glycolysis continues, producing lactate.
Correct: cyanide blocks complex IV, forcing anaerobic metabolism and lactate production.
Oligomycin blocks ATP synthase; uncouplers let protons leak. Neither describes cyanide.
Cyanide does not target PDH; thiamine deficiency impairs PDH.
Hexokinase is not affected by cyanide; glycolysis actually increases.
questions.clue: Enclosed fire, high cyanide, raised lactate.
questions.concept: Respiratory chain inhibition and lactic acidosis.

followUp.q: A body-builder takes 2,4-dinitrophenol to lose weight and develops a very high temperature. What is the mechanism?
options: It carries protons across the inner mitochondrial membrane, bypassing ATP synthase, so energy is released as heat
It activates thermogenin gene expression only in brown fat
followUp.why: 2,4-dinitrophenol is an uncoupler: protons return to the matrix without making ATP, so electron transport races and the energy is lost as heat. It does not block complex IV or act through thermogenin.

questions.q: Calculate the approximate ATP yield from complete aerobic oxidation of one glucose molecule, showing your working. Use P/O ratios of 2.5 for NADH and 1.5 for FADH₂.
markScheme: Glycolysis: net 2 ATP and 2 cytosolic NADH
Cytosolic NADH gives 1.5 or 2.5 ATP each depending on the shuttle (glycerol-3-phosphate or malate–aspartate): 3 or 5 ATP
PDH: 2 NADH = 5 ATP
Krebs cycle (two turns): 6 NADH = 15 ATP; 2 FADH₂ = 3 ATP; 2 GTP = 2 ATP
Total about 30–32 ATP
questions.modelAnswer: Glycolysis gives a net 2 ATP and 2 NADH in the cytosol. That NADH reaches the respiratory chain either through the glycerol-3-phosphate shuttle, which hands electrons to FAD (2 × 1.5 = 3 ATP), or the malate–aspartate shuttle, which regenerates NADH inside the mitochondrion (2 × 2.5 = 5 ATP). Pyruvate dehydrogenase converts both pyruvates to acetyl-CoA, making 2 NADH (5 ATP). Two turns of the Krebs cycle give 6 NADH (15 ATP), 2 FADH₂ (3 ATP) and 2 GTP (2 ATP). The total is 2 + 3 + 5 + 15 + 3 + 2 = 30 ATP with the glycerol-3-phosphate shuttle, or 32 with the malate–aspartate shuttle. These are approximate figures because P/O ratios are not whole numbers and vary with conditions.
questions.concept: ATP accounting across glycolysis, PDH, the Krebs cycle and oxidative phosphorylation.

questions.q: Which enzyme of the urea cycle is X-linked, and its deficiency is the commonest urea cycle disorder?
questions.why: Ornithine transcarbamylase (OTC) deficiency is X-linked and the commonest urea cycle disorder. The other urea cycle defects are autosomal recessive.
optWhy: CPS-I deficiency is autosomal recessive.
NAGS deficiency is autosomal recessive and rare.
Argininosuccinate synthetase deficiency (citrullinaemia) is autosomal recessive.
Arginase deficiency is autosomal recessive and usually presents later with spasticity.
Correct: OTC deficiency is X-linked and the commonest urea cycle disorder.
questions.clue: 'X-linked' and 'commonest'.
questions.concept: Inheritance of urea cycle disorders.

followUp.q: A girl with OTC deficiency has milder, later-onset symptoms than her affected brother. What best explains this?
options: She has two working copies of the gene
OTC is not expressed in females
Random X-inactivation leaves some liver cells with a working OTC allele
followUp.why: Females with one variant allele are mosaic for X-inactivation; liver cells using the normal X make OTC, so disease is usually milder and depends on how skewed inactivation is. She has only one working copy, not two.

questions.q: A 3-day-old boy, well at birth, stops feeding, becomes drowsy and has a seizure. He is tachypnoeic. Plasma ammonia is markedly raised, glucose is normal, the blood gas shows a respiratory alkalosis, plasma citrulline is low and urinary orotic acid is markedly raised. His maternal uncle died as a newborn. Which enzyme is most likely deficient?
questions.why: Hyperammonaemia with low citrulline and high orotic acid places the block at OTC: carbamoyl phosphate cannot combine with ornithine, so it spills into pyrimidine synthesis. A maternal uncle's neonatal death fits X-linked inheritance.
optWhy: CPS-I deficiency also gives low citrulline, but orotic acid is not raised because carbamoyl phosphate is not made.
PKU does not cause neonatal hyperammonaemia; it is detected by newborn screening.
Correct: low citrulline plus high orotic acid points to OTC deficiency.
Argininosuccinate lyase deficiency gives raised citrulline and argininosuccinic acid.
MCAD deficiency causes hypoketotic hypoglycaemia, but glucose is normal here.
questions.clue: Low citrulline, high orotic acid, affected maternal uncle.
questions.concept: Locating a urea cycle block from metabolite pattern.

followUp.q: Another neonate has very high ammonia, low citrulline and normal or low urinary orotic acid. Which enzyme deficiency fits best?
options: Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I (or N-acetylglutamate synthase)
followUp.why: If carbamoyl phosphate is not made (CPS-I deficiency, or lack of its activator N-acetylglutamate), there is none to spill into orotic acid synthesis, so orotic acid is not raised. OTC deficiency raises orotic acid; ASL and arginase defects raise metabolites after citrulline.

questions.q: A 2-year-old has had a vomiting illness and has eaten little for 18 hours. He becomes drowsy. Glucose is 2.0 mmol/L and blood ketones are low. The liver is not enlarged and lactate is normal. Which disorder is most likely?
questions.why: Hypoglycaemia during fasting or illness without the expected ketone rise is hypoketotic hypoglycaemia, the hallmark of a fatty acid oxidation defect such as MCAD deficiency. Without β-oxidation the liver cannot make ketones.
optWhy: Correct: illness plus fasting, hypoglycaemia and low ketones suggest MCAD deficiency.
GSD type I causes fasting hypoglycaemia with high lactate and a large liver.
Ketotic hypoglycaemia, as the name says, comes with high ketones.
PKU does not cause fasting hypoglycaemia.
OTC deficiency causes hyperammonaemia, not hypoketotic hypoglycaemia.
questions.clue: Fasting, low glucose and low ketones.
questions.concept: Fatty acid oxidation and the fasting fuel switch.

followUp.q: A 7-year-old with MCAD deficiency has gastroenteritis and cannot keep food down. What is the key principle of management?
options: Prevent fasting: give an emergency source of glucose (by mouth or intravenously) promptly
followUp.why: The danger in MCAD deficiency is fasting; preventing catabolism with prompt carbohydrate (intravenous glucose if oral intake fails, following the child's emergency plan) is the key principle. High-fat or ketogenic approaches rely on the pathway that does not work.

questions.q: A 38-year-old man has a total cholesterol of 9.8 mmol/L and tendon xanthomas on his Achilles tendons. His father had a myocardial infarction at 46. Which statement about his condition is most accurate?
options: It is most likely a defect in lipoprotein lipase, raising triglycerides
It is caused by a high-fat diet and needs no family testing
It is an autosomal recessive condition, so his children are unlikely to be affected
It is most likely familial hypercholesterolaemia, usually autosomal dominant, from LDL receptor defects that reduce LDL clearance
Statins cannot work because he has no LDL receptors at all
questions.why: Very high total cholesterol, tendon xanthomas and premature coronary disease in a first-degree relative point to familial hypercholesterolaemia. Most cases are autosomal dominant, usually from LDLR variants (also APOB or PCSK9), so LDL is cleared poorly from plasma. Each child has a 50% chance of inheriting it, which is why cascade testing matters.
optWhy: Lipoprotein lipase deficiency raises triglycerides (chylomicrons), not LDL cholesterol with tendon xanthomas.
Tendon xanthomas and premature family coronary disease suggest a genetic cause; NICE recommends DNA and cascade testing.
FH is usually autosomal dominant; each child has a 1 in 2 chance.
Correct: classic FH picture with dominant inheritance and reduced LDL clearance.
Heterozygous FH leaves one working LDLR allele, so treatment that increases receptor activity still helps.
questions.clue: Cholesterol 9.8, tendon xanthomas, father's MI at 46.
questions.concept: Familial hypercholesterolaemia: genetics and LDL clearance.

followUp.q: A family variant in LDLR has been found in a man with FH. His 30-year-old sister has borderline LDL cholesterol. According to NICE CG71, how should her status be decided?
options: By testing for the known family variant
She does not need testing because she is female
followUp.why: NICE CG71 recommends that when a family variant is known, it (rather than LDL cholesterol) is used to identify affected relatives, because LDL ranges overlap between affected and unaffected people. Angiography does not diagnose FH.

questions.q: Describe how the fed and fasted states regulate fatty acid synthesis and β-oxidation, and explain the role of malonyl-CoA.
markScheme: Fed: insulin promotes dephosphorylation and activation of acetyl-CoA carboxylase; citrate activates it
Malonyl-CoA feeds fatty acid synthase and inhibits CPT-I, blocking entry of fatty acids into mitochondria
Fasting: glucagon and AMPK phosphorylate and inhibit acetyl-CoA carboxylase, so malonyl-CoA falls
CPT-I is released, fatty acids enter mitochondria for β-oxidation, and the liver makes ketones
questions.modelAnswer: In the fed state insulin promotes dephosphorylation of acetyl-CoA carboxylase, and plentiful citrate activates it. The enzyme makes malonyl-CoA, which is the building block for fatty acid synthase and also inhibits carnitine palmitoyltransferase I (CPT-I). Because CPT-I controls entry of long-chain fatty acids into mitochondria, newly made fatty acids are not oxidised straight away. In fasting, glucagon (acting through cAMP and protein kinase A) and AMP-activated kinase phosphorylate and inactivate acetyl-CoA carboxylase. Malonyl-CoA falls, CPT-I is released, and fatty acids enter mitochondria for β-oxidation. In the liver much of the resulting acetyl-CoA becomes ketone bodies, which other tissues use as fuel.
questions.concept: Reciprocal control of fat synthesis and oxidation by malonyl-CoA.

questions.q: Which DNA repair pathway is defective in xeroderma pigmentosum?
questions.why: Nucleotide excision repair recognises bulky lesions such as UV-induced pyrimidine dimers, cuts out the damaged stretch and replaces it. Loss of this pathway causes extreme UV sensitivity and very early skin cancers.
optWhy: Mismatch repair defects cause Lynch syndrome and microsatellite instability.
Correct: nucleotide excision repair removes UV damage.
Base excision repair handles single damaged bases, not bulky UV lesions.
Homologous recombination defects (BRCA1/2) raise breast and ovarian cancer risk.
Non-homologous end joining repairs double-strand breaks; its loss causes immunodeficiency syndromes rather than XP.
questions.clue: 'Xeroderma pigmentosum'.
questions.concept: Matching DNA repair pathways to disease.

followUp.q: A 40-year-old has colorectal cancer with high microsatellite instability, and her mother had endometrial cancer at 48. Which pathway is most likely defective in the germline?
followUp.why: High microsatellite instability with early colorectal and endometrial cancers in the family points to Lynch syndrome, a mismatch repair defect. Nucleotide excision repair defects cause XP; homologous recombination defects are associated with BRCA1/2.

questions.q: A coding-strand DNA sequence reads 5′-ATG GCT TGG AAA-3′. A point mutation changes the third codon to TGA. What is the effect on the encoded peptide?
options: Missense: tryptophan is replaced by another amino acid
Frameshift: every codon after the second is changed
questions.why: The mRNA matches the coding strand with U for T: 5′-AUG GCU UGG AAA-3′, encoding Met–Ala–Trp–Lys. Changing TGG to TGA makes the mRNA codon UGA, a stop codon, so translation ends after Met–Ala: a nonsense mutation.
optWhy: A silent change keeps the same amino acid; UGA codes for no amino acid at all.
A missense change needs a new amino acid; UGA is a stop codon.
No bases are deleted; the codon is changed to a stop.
A single base substitution does not change the reading frame.
Correct: UGA is a stop, giving a truncated peptide.
questions.clue: TGG becomes TGA on the coding strand.
questions.concept: Reading codons from the coding strand and classifying mutations.

followUp.q: In the same sequence (5′-ATG GCT TGG AAA-3′), the C in the second codon (GCT) is deleted. What kind of mutation is this?
followUp.why: Deleting one base shifts the reading frame from that point on: the sequence now reads ATG GTT GGA AA..., so all downstream codons change. An in-frame deletion would remove three bases.

questions.q: A 42-year-old woman has a right-sided colon cancer. Immunohistochemistry shows loss of MSH2 and MSH6 staining, with MLH1 and PMS2 retained. Following NICE guidance, what is the most appropriate next step in principle?
options: Test for BRAF V600E and MLH1 promoter hypermethylation before deciding
No further testing: this pattern is always sporadic
Offer germline testing for Lynch syndrome
Repeat the immunohistochemistry in a year
questions.why: NICE HTG430 (formerly DG27) recommends germline testing when MSH2, MSH6 or PMS2 staining is abnormal. MSH6 is lost with MSH2 because the partner protein is unstable on its own. BRAF and methylation testing are for tumours with abnormal MLH1.
optWhy: BRAF and MLH1 methylation testing apply when MLH1 is lost (or MSI is found), not MSH2/MSH6 loss.
MSH2 loss is not explained by MLH1 methylation, so it cannot be assumed sporadic.
Correct: abnormal MSH2/MSH6 leads directly to an offer of germline testing.
Delaying testing gives no benefit and NICE advises testing at diagnosis.
BRCA1/2 are homologous recombination genes, not mismatch repair genes.
questions.clue: MSH2 and MSH6 lost; MLH1 and PMS2 retained.
questions.concept: NICE testing pathway for Lynch syndrome in colorectal cancer.

followUp.q: A 70-year-old's colorectal cancer shows loss of MLH1 and PMS2. According to NICE, what should be tested before germline testing?
options: BRAF V600E, then MLH1 promoter hypermethylation if BRAF is negative
Nothing: go straight to germline testing
followUp.why: With abnormal MLH1, NICE recommends BRAF V600E testing and then MLH1 promoter hypermethylation testing; germline testing follows only if these are negative, because many such tumours are sporadic.

questions.q: A boy has proximal weakness from age 3, a positive Gowers' sign and very high creatine kinase. Testing shows a deletion of exons 48–50 of DMD that shifts the reading frame. His cousin, with a different deletion that keeps the frame, walks independently at 25. What best explains the difference?
options: The boy's frameshift leads to a premature stop and no functional dystrophin; the cousin's in-frame deletion allows a shorter, partly functional dystrophin
The boy's deletion is larger, and severity depends only on size
The cousin's deletion is in a non-coding region
Dystrophin is not involved in the cousin's disease
questions.why: The reading-frame rule: frame-shifting deletions in DMD lead to premature stop codons and absent dystrophin (Duchenne), whereas in-frame deletions keep the frame and produce a shortened protein with some function (Becker). Severity follows the frame more closely than deletion size.
optWhy: Correct: frameshift means no dystrophin; in-frame means a partly working dystrophin.
Size matters less than whether the reading frame is preserved.
The cousin is described as having Becker-type features; nothing suggests a female carrier.
An in-frame exon deletion removes coding sequence; it is not non-coding.
Both have DMD deletions; dystrophin is the protein involved in both.
questions.clue: Frameshifting versus in-frame deletion.
questions.concept: The reading-frame rule in dystrophinopathies.

followUp.q: A newborn's CFTR gene lacks the three bases encoding phenylalanine 508 on both alleles. How should this mutation be classified?
followUp.why: Removing three bases deletes one amino acid without shifting the reading frame: an in-frame deletion. The protein misfolds and is degraded, but it is not truncated by a frameshift or stop.

questions.q: Distinguish a missense, a nonsense and a frameshift mutation, giving a clinical example of each.
markScheme: Missense: single base change replacing one amino acid, e.g. sickle cell disease (β-globin Glu6Val)
Nonsense: single base change creating a premature stop codon, e.g. nonsense variants in DMD
Frameshift: insertion or deletion not divisible by three shifts the reading frame, e.g. frame-shifting DMD deletions (Duchenne)
Contrast with in-frame deletions (e.g. CFTR F508del or Becker-type DMD deletions) that keep the frame
questions.modelAnswer: A missense mutation changes one codon so that a different amino acid is inserted. In sickle cell disease, GAG becomes GTG in codon 6 of β-globin, replacing glutamate with valine; deoxygenated HbS polymerises. A nonsense mutation changes a codon to a premature stop, truncating the protein, and the faulty mRNA is often destroyed by nonsense-mediated decay; some cases of Duchenne muscular dystrophy are caused this way. A frameshift results from inserting or deleting a number of bases not divisible by three, so every downstream codon is read in a new frame, usually reaching an early stop. In DMD, frame-shifting deletions usually give Duchenne disease with no dystrophin, whereas in-frame deletions keep a shorter, partly functional dystrophin and give the milder Becker form. CFTR F508del is another in-frame deletion: one amino acid is lost but the frame is kept.
questions.concept: Classifying mutations by their effect on the reading frame and protein.

questions.q: After a Gq-coupled receptor is activated, which second messenger directly releases Ca²⁺ from the endoplasmic reticulum?
questions.why: Phospholipase C splits PIP₂ into IP₃ and DAG. IP₃ diffuses to IP₃ receptors on the ER and releases stored Ca²⁺; DAG stays in the membrane and, with Ca²⁺, activates protein kinase C.
optWhy: cAMP is the Gs/Gi messenger and activates protein kinase A.
DAG activates protein kinase C; it does not release Ca²⁺ from the ER.
cGMP is made by guanylyl cyclase, for example in response to nitric oxide; it is not the Gq messenger.
Correct: IP₃ opens ER Ca²⁺ channels.
Nitric oxide activates soluble guanylyl cyclase; it is not produced by Gq signalling.
questions.clue: 'Gq' and 'releases Ca²⁺ from the ER'.
questions.concept: Second messengers of the Gq pathway.

followUp.q: Which enzyme is activated by cAMP after a Gs-coupled receptor is stimulated?
followUp.why: cAMP binds the regulatory subunits of protein kinase A, freeing its catalytic subunits. Protein kinase C is activated by DAG and Ca²⁺; phospholipase C is the Gq effector; JAK2 serves cytokine receptors.

questions.q: A 30-year-old aid worker returns from a cholera outbreak and passes many litres of painless, pale watery stool without blood. Stool microscopy shows no white cells. Which mechanism explains the diarrhoea?
options: Destruction of the intestinal villi by bacterial invasion
Toxin-mediated activation of Gsα that cannot be switched off, raising cAMP and opening CFTR
Blocking of SGLT1 so sodium cannot be absorbed
Inhibition of Gq, lowering intracellular Ca²⁺
Toxin-mediated inactivation of Gi in the gut
questions.why: Cholera toxin ADP-ribosylates Gsα so it cannot hydrolyse its GTP. Adenylyl cyclase stays on, cAMP stays high, protein kinase A opens CFTR, and chloride and water pour into the lumen. The mucosa is intact, so there is no blood or white cells.
optWhy: Invasion would cause inflammation, blood and white cells in the stool; cholera is non-invasive.
Correct: Gsα stuck in its active state drives cAMP-dependent chloride secretion.
SGLT1 still works in cholera, which is why oral rehydration solution is effective.
Cholera does not act on Gq.
Inactivating Gi describes pertussis toxin, not cholera toxin.
questions.clue: Painless, bloodless, very high-volume stool after cholera exposure.
questions.concept: G protein signalling disrupted by cholera toxin.

followUp.q: Why can oral rehydration solution, which contains glucose and sodium, replace losses in cholera?
options: Glucose–sodium co-transport (SGLT1) is still working, so water is absorbed with them
followUp.why: SGLT1 is unaffected by the toxin. Absorbing glucose with sodium draws water back in osmotically, outweighing ongoing secretion. ORS does not block CFTR, kill the organism or lower cAMP.

questions.q: A tumour cell line has lost both copies of RB1. Which change in cell-cycle control would you expect?
options: Cyclin D can no longer be made
Cells cannot enter mitosis because CDK1 is absent
E2F is no longer held in check, so cells pass the G1/S restriction point without the usual mitogen signals
questions.why: Unphosphorylated Rb normally binds E2F and blocks S-phase genes until cyclin D–CDK4/6 phosphorylates it. Without Rb, E2F is free, so cells enter S phase without the usual growth-factor control: a classic tumour suppressor loss.
optWhy: Loss of a brake would cause uncontrolled entry, not arrest.
Cyclin D is still made; it simply has no Rb target to control the restriction point.
RB1 loss does not remove CDK1; mitosis still proceeds.
TP53 is a separate gene; RB1 loss does not stop p53 being made.
Correct: free E2F drives S-phase entry without the normal checks.
questions.clue: Both RB1 copies lost.
questions.concept: Rb and E2F at the G1/S restriction point.

followUp.q: Why might a CDK4/6 inhibitor work poorly in a breast cancer that has lost Rb?
options: Their effect depends on keeping Rb unphosphorylated; without Rb, E2F is already free
CDK4/6 inhibitors work only by blocking p53
Rb-negative cells lack cyclin D receptors
CDK4/6 inhibitors need Rb to enter the cell
followUp.why: CDK4/6 inhibitors stop cells passing the restriction point by preventing Rb phosphorylation. If Rb is absent, E2F is free regardless, so blocking CDK4/6 has little effect on that checkpoint.

questions.q: A 14-month-old has retinoblastoma in both eyes. Her father had a retinoblastoma removed in infancy. Which statement best explains this pattern?
options: Retinoblastoma is caused by an oncogene, so one somatic mutation is enough in anyone
Both her RB1 alleles were inherited in a mutated form
She inherited one inactivated RB1 allele; a single somatic hit in a retinal cell then causes a tumour, so tumours are early and bilateral
Bilateral disease shows the cancer spread from one eye to the other
questions.why: Knudson's two-hit hypothesis: RB1 is a tumour suppressor, so both alleles must be lost for a tumour. In hereditary retinoblastoma the first hit is inherited and present in every cell, so only one more hit is needed. This makes tumours earlier, often bilateral and multiple. The pattern is passed on as an autosomal dominant predisposition.
optWhy: RB1 is a tumour suppressor, not an oncogene; both copies must be lost in the tumour.
Two inherited mutant alleles would be very unlikely; one inherited hit plus a somatic one explains the pattern.
Correct: one inherited hit plus one somatic hit per tumour.
Bilateral retinoblastoma reflects independent tumours, not spread between eyes.
Her father passed it to her, and RB1 predisposition is autosomal dominant, not X-linked.
questions.clue: Bilateral, early, affected father.
questions.concept: Knudson's two-hit hypothesis for tumour suppressors.

followUp.q: Sporadic (non-inherited) retinoblastoma is usually unilateral and occurs later. Why?
options: Sporadic cases need two somatic hits in the same retinal cell, which is a rarer event
Sporadic cases are caused by infection
Sporadic cases need only one hit
followUp.why: Without an inherited first hit, two independent somatic hits must occur in the same cell, which is much less likely, so tumours are usually single and appear later.

questions.q: Explain how the retinoblastoma protein (Rb) and p53 control the G1/S transition, and how loss of each contributes to cancer.
markScheme: Unphosphorylated Rb binds E2F, blocking S-phase gene transcription
Mitogens induce cyclin D–CDK4/6 (then cyclin E–CDK2), which phosphorylate Rb and release E2F
DNA damage stabilises p53 (normally degraded via MDM2); p53 induces p21, a CDK inhibitor, keeping Rb unphosphorylated and arresting the cell
Severe damage leads p53 to trigger apoptosis
Loss of Rb removes the restriction point; loss of p53 lets damaged cells keep dividing and accumulate mutations (two-hit tumour suppressors)
questions.modelAnswer: Rb guards the restriction point in G1. In its unphosphorylated form it binds the E2F transcription factors and holds back the genes needed for DNA synthesis. Growth factors induce cyclin D, which activates CDK4 and CDK6; these, followed by cyclin E–CDK2, phosphorylate Rb and release E2F, committing the cell to S phase. p53 is normally kept low because MDM2 targets it for breakdown. DNA damage stabilises p53, which switches on p21, a CDK inhibitor. Rb therefore stays unphosphorylated and the cell pauses at G1/S while it repairs. If the damage is too great, p53 instead promotes apoptosis. Both are tumour suppressors: both alleles must be lost (Knudson's two hits). Without Rb, cells enter S phase without proper mitogen control; without p53, damaged cells neither stop nor die, so mutations accumulate.
questions.concept: Rb, E2F, p53 and p21 at the G1/S checkpoint.

questions.q: Which pedigree feature excludes X-linked inheritance?
options: An affected father has an affected son
An unaffected mother has an affected son
Females are more mildly affected than males
questions.why: A father passes his Y chromosome, not his X, to his sons, so an affected father with an affected son (male-to-male transmission) rules out X-linked inheritance.
optWhy: Correct: male-to-male transmission cannot happen through the X chromosome.
Only affected males is typical of X-linked recessive inheritance; it does not exclude it.
An unaffected carrier mother with an affected son is the classic X-linked recessive pattern.
Skipping generations fits recessive (including X-linked recessive) inheritance.
Milder disease in females fits X-linked conditions with variable X-inactivation.
questions.clue: 'Excludes X-linked'.
questions.concept: Male-to-male transmission and the X chromosome.

followUp.q: Which pedigree feature is most typical of mitochondrial (mtDNA) inheritance?
options: Affected men pass the condition to all their children
Affected women can pass it to children of both sexes; affected men do not pass it on
One in four children affected when both parents are carriers
followUp.why: mtDNA comes from the egg, so transmission is through the mother to sons and daughters, not from father to child. One in four with carrier parents describes autosomal recessive inheritance.

questions.q: A couple's first child has cystic fibrosis. Their unaffected 25-year-old daughter asks what her chance is of being a carrier. What is it?
questions.why: Both parents must be carriers. Their children are AA, Aa, aA or aa with equal probability. Because she is unaffected, aa is excluded, and two of the three remaining genotypes are carriers: 2/3.
optWhy: 1/4 is the chance of a child being affected when both parents are carriers, not the carrier risk of an unaffected sibling.
1/2 is the carrier risk for any child before excluding the affected genotype.
3/4 is the chance of being unaffected, not of being a carrier.
Correct: 2 of the 3 unaffected genotypes are carriers.
She could be a non-carrier (AA), so the risk is not certain.
questions.clue: Unaffected sibling of an affected child; recessive condition.
questions.concept: Conditional (2/3) carrier risk for unaffected siblings.

followUp.q: If that daughter (carrier risk 2/3) has a child with an unrelated partner whose carrier risk is 1/25, what is the risk the child has cystic fibrosis?
followUp.why: Risk = 2/3 × 1/25 × 1/4 = 2/300 = 1/150. 1/100 treats her as a certain carrier (1 × 1/25 × 1/4); 1/200 uses 1/2 instead of 2/3 for her carrier risk (1/2 × 1/25 × 1/4); 1/600 applies the 1/4 twice.

questions.q: A recessive disorder affects 1 in 3,600 births in a population at Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium. What is the approximate carrier frequency?
questions.why: q² = 1/3,600, so q = 1/60 and p = 59/60. Carrier frequency 2pq = 2 × 59/60 × 1/60 ≈ 1/30.5, about 1 in 30. Because p is close to 1, 2q (2/60) is a good shortcut.
optWhy: 1 in 60 is the allele frequency q, not the carrier frequency 2pq.
Correct: 2pq ≈ 2 × 1/60 ≈ 1 in 30.
1 in 120 uses q/2 instead of 2q.
1 in 1,800 doubles the disease frequency (2q²) rather than using 2pq.
1 in 3,600 is the frequency of affected homozygotes (q²).
questions.clue: Incidence 1 in 3,600, recessive, Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium.
questions.concept: Hardy–Weinberg carrier frequency from disease incidence.

followUp.q: In another population, 1 in 100 people carries a recessive allele. Assuming random mating, roughly what is the birth incidence of the disease?
followUp.why: Carrier frequency 2pq ≈ 2q = 1/100, so q ≈ 1/200 and q² ≈ 1/40,000. Equivalently, the chance two carriers meet is 1/100 × 1/100 and a quarter of their children are affected: 1/40,000. 1 in 10,000 forgets the 1/4.

questions.q: A baby has floppiness and poor feeding at birth, and later develops overeating and obesity. Genetic testing shows two maternal copies of chromosome 15 and no paternal copy. What is the diagnosis and mechanism?
options: Angelman syndrome caused by maternal uniparental disomy
Prader–Willi syndrome caused by a maternal deletion
Fragile X syndrome from a CGG repeat expansion
Prader–Willi syndrome caused by maternal uniparental disomy, losing paternally expressed genes at 15q11–q13
questions.why: Genes at 15q11–q13 are imprinted. Prader–Willi syndrome results from loss of the paternal contribution: a paternal deletion (about 60%) or maternal uniparental disomy (about 30%), as here. Neonatal hypotonia and poor feeding followed by hyperphagia is the typical course.
optWhy: Angelman syndrome comes from loss of the maternal contribution (maternal deletion or paternal UPD).
A maternal deletion causes Angelman, not Prader–Willi.
Trisomy 21 is a different chromosome and a different picture.
Fragile X involves an X-linked CGG repeat and does not explain UPD 15.
Correct: maternal UPD means no paternal 15q11–q13 expression, causing Prader–Willi.
questions.clue: Two maternal copies of chromosome 15.
questions.concept: Genomic imprinting at 15q11–q13.

followUp.q: A child with severe learning disability, absent speech, ataxia and a happy demeanour has a deletion of 15q11–q13 on the chromosome inherited from the mother. What is the diagnosis?
followUp.why: Loss of the maternal contribution at 15q11–q13 causes Angelman syndrome; the same deletion on the paternal chromosome would cause Prader–Willi.

questions.q: Using Hardy–Weinberg, a recessive disorder affects 1 in 2,500 births. Calculate the allele frequency and carrier frequency, and state two assumptions of the calculation.
markScheme: Carrier frequency 2pq = 2 × 49/50 × 1/50 ≈ 1/25.5 (about 1 in 25; 2q shortcut gives 1/25)
Assumptions: large, randomly mating population; no selection, mutation or migration (any two)
questions.modelAnswer: The frequency of affected homozygotes is q² = 1/2,500, so the disease allele frequency is q = √(1/2,500) = 1/50. The normal allele frequency is p = 1 − 1/50 = 49/50. The carrier frequency is 2pq = 2 × (49/50) × (1/50) = 98/2,500 ≈ 0.039, or about 1 in 25. Because p is close to 1, 2q gives a quick estimate (2/50 = 1/25). The calculation assumes Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium: a large population with random mating and no selection, mutation, migration or genetic drift changing allele frequencies.
questions.concept: Hardy–Weinberg calculation of allele and carrier frequencies.

questions.q: A 24-year-old man of Mediterranean ancestry develops dark urine, jaundice and fatigue three days after starting an antimalarial for travel prophylaxis. Haemoglobin has fallen from 148 to 96 g/L, reticulocytes are raised, and the blood film shows bite cells and, with supravital staining, Heinz bodies. Explain the biochemical basis of this presentation, linking the pentose phosphate pathway to red cell survival, and discuss how the diagnosis would be confirmed and the principles of management.
markScheme: Likely G6PD deficiency (X-linked, so males with one variant allele are affected) triggered by an oxidant drug such as primaquine
G6PD catalyses the first, rate-limiting step of the oxidative pentose phosphate pathway, making NADPH
Mature red cells lack mitochondria and nuclei; the pentose phosphate pathway is their main NADPH source and they cannot make new enzyme
NADPH keeps glutathione reduced (glutathione reductase); reduced glutathione removes hydrogen peroxide (glutathione peroxidase)
Oxidant stress denatures haemoglobin, which precipitates as Heinz bodies; splenic macrophages remove them, leaving bite cells
Intravascular and extravascular haemolysis: dark urine, unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia, raised LDH, low haptoglobin, reticulocytosis
Other triggers: infection, fava beans and other drugs (e.g. dapsone, rasburicase, some sulfonamides)
Confirm with a G6PD assay; testing during haemolysis can be falsely normal, so repeat after recovery if suspicion remains
Management principles: stop the trigger, supportive care, transfusion if severe, education on drugs and foods to avoid; test G6PD before high-risk drugs
questions.modelAnswer:
The picture is acute haemolysis after an oxidant drug in a young man of Mediterranean ancestry, which points to glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency. The gene lies on the X chromosome, so a male with one variant allele is affected. The 8-aminoquinoline antimalarials such as primaquine are classic triggers.

G6PD catalyses the first, rate-limiting step of the oxidative pentose phosphate pathway, oxidising glucose-6-phosphate and reducing NADP⁺ to NADPH. Mature red cells have no mitochondria and no nucleus. The pentose phosphate pathway is their main source of NADPH, and they cannot replace enzyme that is lost as the cell ages. NADPH is used by glutathione reductase to keep glutathione in its reduced form, and glutathione peroxidase uses reduced glutathione to break down hydrogen peroxide and other oxidants.

With reduced G6PD activity, everyday life is usually symptom-free. An oxidant load from a drug, fava beans or infection overwhelms the cell. Haemoglobin is oxidised and the denatured globin precipitates as Heinz bodies attached to the membrane, and membrane lipids and proteins are damaged. Some cells lyse in the circulation, releasing haemoglobin that darkens the urine and is mopped up by haptoglobin, so haptoglobin falls. Others pass through the spleen, where macrophages pluck out Heinz bodies, leaving bite cells, or remove whole cells. Haem breakdown raises unconjugated bilirubin, causing jaundice, and LDH rises. The marrow responds with a reticulocytosis. Episodes are often self-limiting, because young red cells have more enzyme.

Diagnosis is confirmed by a G6PD assay. During acute haemolysis the oldest, most deficient cells have already been destroyed and the remaining young cells have more enzyme, so a result can be falsely normal; if suspicion remains, the test is repeated after recovery. A negative direct antiglobulin test helps exclude immune haemolysis.

Management is to stop the trigger and give supportive care, including hydration and monitoring of haemoglobin and kidney function; transfusion is considered if anaemia is severe. He should be told which drugs and foods to avoid and that infections can also trigger episodes. More widely, G6PD status should be checked before prescribing high-risk drugs such as primaquine, tafenoquine or rasburicase. No doses are given here.
questions.concept: G6PD, NADPH and glutathione in red cell defence against oxidants.

questions.q: Ruth, aged 42, is diagnosed with colorectal cancer at the hepatic flexure. Her mother had endometrial cancer at 48 and her maternal uncle had colorectal cancer at 45. Immunohistochemistry on Ruth's tumour shows loss of MSH2 and MSH6, and the tumour has high microsatellite instability. Explain the molecular basis of these findings, the pattern of inheritance, the UK testing pathway, and the implications for Ruth and her relatives.
markScheme: Likely Lynch syndrome: a germline mismatch repair (MMR) variant, here most likely MSH2 (MSH6 lost as its unstable partner), or an EPCAM deletion silencing MSH2
MMR corrects base mismatches and insertion–deletion loops from polymerase slippage, especially at microsatellites
MSH2–MSH6 recognises errors; MLH1–PMS2 is recruited to remove and resynthesise the faulty stretch
Two-hit model: germline variant in every cell, plus somatic loss of the second allele in the tumour
MMR deficiency causes accumulated mutations, high microsatellite instability and many neoantigens
Autosomal dominant with incomplete penetrance; colorectal (often right-sided), endometrial, ovarian, stomach, small bowel and urinary tract cancers
NICE HTG430 (formerly DG27): test all colorectal cancers at diagnosis by MMR IHC or MSI; MLH1 loss goes to BRAF V600E and MLH1 methylation testing; MSH2/MSH6/PMS2 loss goes to germline testing
MMR-deficient tumours tend to respond to immune checkpoint inhibitors (high neoantigen load), relevant to oncology decisions
Relatives: genetic counselling, predictive testing for the family variant, 1 in 2 risk to first-degree relatives; carriers offered surveillance and risk-reduction discussion
questions.modelAnswer:
Ruth's tumour has the hallmarks of Lynch syndrome: early-onset, right-sided colorectal cancer, close relatives with colorectal and endometrial cancer across two generations, loss of MSH2 and MSH6 staining and high microsatellite instability.

DNA mismatch repair corrects errors that escape polymerase proofreading. These are mainly single mismatched bases and small loops made when the polymerase slips on short repeated sequences (microsatellites). A complex of MSH2 and MSH6 recognises the error; MLH1 and PMS2 are then recruited, the newly made strand is cut, and the stretch is resynthesised. The partner proteins are unstable when alone, so loss of MSH2 brings loss of MSH6 on immunohistochemistry. Ruth's pattern therefore points to a defect in MSH2, or less often an EPCAM deletion that switches off the neighbouring MSH2 gene.

In Lynch syndrome every cell carries one pathogenic germline variant. A tumour forms when the second copy is lost in a cell, in keeping with Knudson's two-hit model. Repair-deficient cells accumulate mutations, especially at microsatellites, giving high microsatellite instability and many abnormal proteins (neoantigens). Inheritance is autosomal dominant with high but incomplete penetrance, which fits the maternal-side family history. Associated cancers include colorectal (often proximal), endometrial, ovarian, gastric, small bowel and upper urinary tract cancers.

In the UK, NICE HTG430 (formerly DG27) recommends that everyone with colorectal cancer is tested at diagnosis with MMR immunohistochemistry or MSI testing, without delaying treatment. Where MLH1 is lost, BRAF V600E and then MLH1 promoter hypermethylation testing are done first, because these usually mean a sporadic tumour. Where MSH2, MSH6 or PMS2 is lost, as for Ruth, germline testing is offered.

For Ruth's treatment, MMR-deficient tumours carry a high neoantigen load and tend to respond to immune checkpoint inhibitors, which oncologists consider in appropriate settings; this is specialist practice and no doses are given here.

If a germline variant is confirmed, each of her first-degree relatives has a 1 in 2 chance of carrying it. They should be offered genetic counselling and predictive testing for the family variant, explained by suitably trained staff. Carriers are offered regular colonoscopic surveillance and, for women, a discussion of gynaecological risk reduction, following specialist advice.
questions.concept: Mismatch repair, microsatellite instability and the NICE Lynch testing pathway.

cases.title: A floppy baby before the next feed

steps.text: A 5-month-old girl is brought in after a seizure early in the morning, about 6 hours after her last feed. She has had several sweaty, irritable episodes before feeds. On examination she has a round face and a liver edge 5 cm below the costal margin. Capillary glucose is 1.5 mmol/L.

ask.q: Before glucose is given, which samples taken now would most help find the cause of the hypoglycaemia?
options: Blood ketones, lactate, insulin, free fatty acids and acylcarnitines with a stored 'hypoglycaemia screen' sample
ask.why: Samples taken at the time of hypoglycaemia show which fuel system has failed: ketones and fatty acids test fat oxidation, lactate points to gluconeogenic or glycogen defects, insulin excludes hyperinsulinism and acylcarnitines screen for fatty acid oxidation disorders. Once glucose is given, these clues disappear. A blood count, thyroid tests or chest X-ray do not explain a fasting hypoglycaemia with a big liver.

steps.text: Results from the critical sample: glucose 1.5 mmol/L, lactate 7.5 mmol/L (high), blood ketones only mildly raised, insulin suppressed, urate and triglycerides raised. Acylcarnitine profile is normal.

options: Glycogen storage disease type I (glucose-6-phosphatase system)
ask.why: Hepatomegaly with fasting hypoglycaemia, marked lactic acidosis, hyperuricaemia and hyperlipidaemia is classic GSD type I. Insulin is appropriately suppressed (not hyperinsulinism), the acylcarnitine profile is normal and the marked lactic acidosis with a big liver is not typical of MCAD deficiency, and McArdle disease affects muscle, not blood glucose.

steps.text: Genetic testing confirms biallelic G6PC1 variants. Her parents are both unaffected carriers.

ask.q: Why is lactate so high in this condition?
options: Her muscles are exercising during seizures only
Glucose-6-phosphate that cannot become free glucose is pushed down glycolysis to pyruvate and lactate
ask.why: Glucose-6-phosphate builds up in the liver because it cannot be dephosphorylated. It is diverted into glycolysis, producing pyruvate and lactate, and into lipid and urate synthesis, explaining the whole biochemical pattern. Seizures can add some lactate but do not explain a persistent pattern.

steps.text: Outcome: she is managed by a specialist metabolic team with frequent feeds and avoidance of fasting to keep glucose up, with monitoring of growth, liver, kidneys and lipids. Her parents receive genetic counselling: each future pregnancy has a 1 in 4 chance of being affected.

debrief: Take a critical sample (glucose, ketones, lactate, insulin, fatty acids, acylcarnitines) at the time of hypoglycaemia, before treating, when possible.
Fasting hypoglycaemia with hepatomegaly and lactic acidosis suggests glycogen storage disease type I.
Glucose-6-phosphatase is the final step for both glycogen breakdown and gluconeogenesis, so both routes to blood glucose fail.
Autosomal recessive conditions carry a 1 in 4 recurrence risk when both parents are carriers.

cases.title: High cholesterol and a family history

steps.text: A 38-year-old electrician has a health check. His total cholesterol is 9.8 mmol/L with LDL cholesterol 7.6 mmol/L and normal triglycerides. He feels well and does not smoke.

ask.q: What is the most useful next piece of information?
options: His family history of premature coronary heart disease and raised cholesterol, plus examination for tendon xanthomas
ask.why: NICE CG71 asks clinicians to consider FH when cholesterol is high (total cholesterol typically above 7.5 mmol/L), especially with a personal or family history of premature coronary disease. The Simon Broome criteria combine cholesterol levels, family history, tendon xanthomas and DNA results. The other options do not help.

steps.text: His father had a myocardial infarction at 46 and his paternal aunt is on lipid-lowering treatment. Examination shows thickened Achilles tendons with xanthomas. TSH, liver and kidney function are normal.

options: A clinical diagnosis of familial hypercholesterolaemia, to be confirmed with a DNA test
ask.why: Tendon xanthomas with very high cholesterol meet the clinical picture of definite FH under the Simon Broome criteria; NICE recommends offering a DNA test to confirm it and to allow testing of relatives. Normal TSH and liver and kidney function exclude common secondary causes.

steps.text: DNA testing finds a pathogenic LDLR variant. He has a 9-year-old daughter and a 12-year-old son, and two brothers.

ask.q: What is each of his children's chance of having inherited the variant, and what should happen?
options: 1 in 2; offer cascade testing for the family variant
Almost none, because FH skips generations
Only his son is at risk because it is X-linked
ask.why: Heterozygous FH from an LDLR variant is autosomal dominant, so each child has a 1 in 2 chance. NICE CG71 recommends cascade testing of first- and second-degree (and when possible third-degree) relatives, using the family variant once known. It does not skip generations and is not X-linked.

steps.text: Outcome: he starts lipid-lowering treatment under specialist advice (doses are not covered here) with lifestyle support. His brothers and children are offered testing for the family variant; his daughter carries it and is referred to a paediatric lipid service.

debrief: Very high LDL cholesterol with tendon xanthomas and premature coronary disease in the family suggests familial hypercholesterolaemia.
Most FH is autosomal dominant (usually LDLR), so first-degree relatives have a 50% chance of being affected.
NICE CG71: diagnose with the Simon Broome criteria, offer DNA testing, and cascade-test relatives using the family variant once known.
Exclude secondary causes such as hypothyroidism, and liver and kidney disease.

cases.title: A brother with Duchenne

steps.text: Sophie, 28, is planning a pregnancy. Her brother had Duchenne muscular dystrophy and died at 22. Her parents are unaffected; no one else in the family is known to be affected.

ask.q: What is the mode of inheritance of Duchenne muscular dystrophy?
ask.why: DMD is X-linked recessive: the DMD gene (dystrophin) is on the X chromosome, so males with one variant are affected, while females are usually unaffected carriers. Fathers do not pass it to sons.

steps.text: Her mother's creatine kinase is raised, and testing finds that her mother carries the frame-shifting DMD deletion that her brother had.

ask.q: Before any test of Sophie herself, what is her chance of being a carrier?
ask.why: Her mother is a confirmed carrier, so Sophie had a 1 in 2 chance of inheriting the X with the deletion. The 2/3 figure applies to unaffected siblings in autosomal recessive conditions, not here.

steps.text: Targeted testing for the family deletion shows that Sophie is a carrier. Her partner is unaffected.

ask.q: What are the risks for each of her pregnancies?
options: Each son 1 in 2 affected; each daughter 1 in 2 a carrier
Each child 1 in 4 affected regardless of sex
No risk, because her partner is unaffected
ask.why: Each child receives one of her two X chromosomes. A son who receives the variant X is affected (1 in 2 sons); a daughter who receives it is a carrier (1 in 2 daughters). For a pregnancy of unknown sex, the chance of an affected son is 1 in 4.

steps.text: Outcome: Sophie receives genetic counselling about reproductive options, which can include prenatal diagnosis and preimplantation genetic testing. Because some female carriers develop heart muscle disease, she is also offered cardiac assessment.

debrief: DMD is X-linked recessive; daughters of a carrier mother each have a 1 in 2 chance of being carriers.
A carrier's sons each have a 1 in 2 chance of being affected; for a pregnancy of unknown sex, 1 in 4 of an affected son.
Confirm carrier status with targeted testing for the known family variant.
Some carriers have symptoms from skewed X-inactivation, including cardiomyopathy, so cardiac review is offered.

interpret.title: Potassium and the membrane potential
rows: 133–146 (typical adult UK range; varies by lab)
3.5–5.3 (typical adult UK range; varies by lab)
2.5–7.8 (typical adult UK range; varies by lab)
60–120 (typical adult UK range; varies by lab)
interpret.q: A 72-year-old with acute kidney injury has these results; the sample was not haemolysed. Taking intracellular K⁺ as 140 mmol/L, what is the approximate K⁺ equilibrium potential, and what does it mean for his myocytes?
options: About −95 mV: no change from normal
About −110 mV: myocytes are hyperpolarised and less excitable
About −80 mV: myocytes are depolarised, risking slowed conduction and arrhythmia
About −40 mV: myocytes are at threshold
interpret.why: E_K = 61.5 × log₁₀(7/140) = 61.5 × −1.301 ≈ −80 mV, about 15 mV less negative than at a normal K⁺ of 4 mmol/L (−95 mV). Myocytes depolarise; sustained depolarisation inactivates Na⁺ channels, slowing conduction, so this level is dangerous and needs urgent attention. Poor renal excretion (high urea and creatinine) explains the rise.
optWhy: −95 mV is E_K at a plasma K⁺ of 4 mmol/L, not 7.
A positive E_K would need plasma K⁺ above intracellular K⁺; the sign is wrong.
Hyperpolarisation happens when plasma K⁺ falls, not when it rises.
Correct: 61.5 × log₁₀(7/140) ≈ −80 mV, a depolarising shift.
−40 mV would need plasma K⁺ of roughly 31 mmol/L, far above this value.

interpret.title: Rescued from a house fire
rows: 7.35–7.45 (typical adult UK range; varies by lab)
interpret.q: A 45-year-old rescued from a house fire has a headache and confusion. These are his arterial blood gas results on air. Which interpretation is best?
options: Normal oxygenation: the PaO₂ and SpO₂ are reassuring
Metabolic (lactic) acidosis with partial respiratory compensation; carbon monoxide is reducing O₂ content and delivery despite a normal PaO₂
Primary respiratory acidosis from smoke inhalation
interpret.why: pH is low with low bicarbonate, so this is a metabolic acidosis; PaCO₂ is low because he is breathing more to compensate (check: 6.1 + log₁₀(15/(0.0307 × 30)) ≈ 7.31). The raised lactate shows tissue hypoxia. Carboxyhaemoglobin 25% means a quarter of haem cannot carry O₂, and the rest holds O₂ more tightly (left shift). PaO₂ measures dissolved O₂, and standard oximeters read carboxyhaemoglobin as oxyhaemoglobin, so both look normal.
optWhy: PaO₂ and SpO₂ do not measure carboxyhaemoglobin; the lactate and acidosis show tissue hypoxia.
Correct: low pH and bicarbonate with a compensatory low PaCO₂, raised lactate and a high carboxyhaemoglobin.
Respiratory acidosis needs a high PaCO₂; here it is low.
Respiratory alkalosis needs a high pH; here the pH is low.
Metabolic alkalosis would show a high bicarbonate and high pH.

interpret.title: Dark urine after a new tablet
rows: 130–180 (adult male; typical UK range, varies by lab)
about 20–100 (typical adult range; varies by lab)
interpret.q: A 24-year-old man of Mediterranean ancestry has dark urine three days after starting primaquine. Which interpretation fits these results best?
options: Hepatitis: raised bilirubin from liver cell damage
Haemolysis, not antibody-mediated, most likely oxidant-induced in G6PD deficiency
interpret.why: Low haemoglobin with raised reticulocytes, raised bilirubin and LDH and an undetectable haptoglobin (which binds free haemoglobin) is haemolysis. A negative direct antiglobulin test argues against an immune cause, and the timing after an oxidant drug in a man points to G6PD deficiency. ALT is normal, so the bilirubin is not from hepatitis.
optWhy: ALT is normal; the raised bilirubin comes with low haptoglobin and raised reticulocytes, a haemolytic picture.
Gilbert syndrome raises unconjugated bilirubin mildly without anaemia, reticulocytosis or low haptoglobin.
Autoimmune haemolysis usually gives a positive direct antiglobulin test.
Iron deficiency gives a low reticulocyte response and no raised bilirubin or LDH.
Correct: haemolytic pattern with a negative DAT after an oxidant drug.

interpret.title: A drowsy, fast-breathing newborn
rows: under about 100 in neonates (varies by lab)
interpret.q: A 3-day-old boy who was well at birth is drowsy and breathing fast. His chest X-ray is clear. Which interpretation fits best?
options: Respiratory alkalosis driven by hyperammonaemia, suggesting a urea cycle disorder
interpret.why: pH is high and PaCO₂ low, so this is a respiratory alkalosis; bicarbonate is slightly low as expected renal compensation (check: 6.1 + log₁₀(19/(0.0307 × 22.5)) ≈ 7.54). With a clear chest and normal glucose, a very high ammonia explains it: ammonia stimulates the respiratory centre. This pattern in a neonate suggests a urea cycle disorder such as OTC deficiency.
optWhy: Metabolic acidosis needs a low pH; here pH is high.
Respiratory acidosis needs a high PaCO₂.
Correct: high pH, low PaCO₂ and a very high ammonia.
Metabolic alkalosis would show a raised bicarbonate, not a low one.
pH, PaCO₂ and ammonia are all clearly abnormal.

interpret.title: A fasting lipid profile
rows: ideally under 5 (UK target, not a range)
interpret.q: A 38-year-old man has these results. He has Achilles tendon xanthomas and his father had a myocardial infarction at 46. What is the most likely explanation and next step in principle?
options: Familial hypercholesterolaemia; use Simon Broome criteria, offer DNA testing and cascade testing of relatives (NICE CG71)
Mixed hyperlipidaemia from diet; no family tests needed
Secondary hypercholesterolaemia from hypothyroidism; treat the thyroid
Familial chylomicronaemia from lipoprotein lipase deficiency
interpret.why: Isolated very high LDL cholesterol (triglycerides normal) with tendon xanthomas and premature coronary disease in a first-degree relative is classic FH. TSH is normal, excluding hypothyroidism as a secondary cause. NICE CG71 recommends a clinical diagnosis using the Simon Broome criteria, a DNA test, and cascade testing of relatives.
optWhy: Correct: FH, identified and confirmed as NICE CG71 recommends.
Triglycerides are normal, so this is not a mixed picture; tendon xanthomas and the family history point to a genetic cause.
TSH is normal, so hypothyroidism does not explain the raised cholesterol.
Lipoprotein lipase deficiency causes very high triglycerides, not isolated high LDL.
Total cholesterol 9.8 and LDL 7.6 mmol/L are markedly raised.

interpret.title: Rice-water stools
rows: 133–146 (typical adult UK range; varies by lab)
interpret.q: A 30-year-old with cholera has these results. Calculate the anion gap. Which interpretation fits?
options: Anion gap 40 mmol/L: lactic acidosis only
Anion gap 30 mmol/L: high anion gap acidosis from ketones
Anion gap 14 mmol/L: metabolic alkalosis from vomiting
Anion gap 14 mmol/L: normal anion gap metabolic acidosis from stool bicarbonate loss, with hypokalaemia and dehydration
interpret.why: Anion gap = Na − (Cl + HCO₃) = 136 − (108 + 14) = 14 mmol/L, within the usual range (roughly 8–16 by this formula; varies by lab). Low bicarbonate with a normal gap fits loss of bicarbonate-rich stool, with chloride retained. Low potassium reflects stool losses, and raised urea and creatinine show dehydration (prerenal).
optWhy: 40 is arithmetically wrong; a severe lactic acidosis would raise the gap, which is normal here.
30 does not follow from these values, and ketones are not the main problem here.
Bicarbonate is low, so this is an acidosis, not an alkalosis.
Correct: 136 − 122 = 14, a normal-gap acidosis from bicarbonate loss.
Bicarbonate 14 mmol/L is clearly abnormal.

interpret.title: A boy who climbs up his legs
rows: under about 200–300 in children (varies by lab and age)
interpret.q: A 4-year-old boy is slow to run, falls often and rises from the floor by pushing on his thighs. Which interpretation fits best?
options: Liver disease, because ALT and AST are raised
A muscle disorder such as Duchenne muscular dystrophy; the raised ALT and AST come from muscle
interpret.why: A creatine kinase many times the upper limit with proximal weakness and a Gowers' manoeuvre points to a dystrophinopathy. ALT and AST are also found in muscle, so they rise with muscle damage; a normal bilirubin and the very high CK argue against liver disease. TSH is normal. The next step is genetic testing of DMD (deletion/duplication analysis, then sequencing).
optWhy: ALT and AST can come from muscle; with a CK of 18,500 U/L, muscle is the likely source.
Correct: very high CK with proximal weakness suggests a dystrophinopathy.
TSH is normal, so hypothyroidism is not the cause.
A CK of 18,500 U/L is far above the normal range for a child.
Haemolysis would show anaemia and raised bilirubin, not a CK this high.
